title_en: How AI decision models could change content moderation
title_fa: How AI decision models could change content moderation
excerpt_en: On Tuesday, Musubi announced a lightweight decision model made for real-time moderation called PolicyLM-1.7B, released with open weights.
excerpt_fa: On Tuesday, Musubi announced a lightweight decision model made for real-time moderation called PolicyLM-1.7B, released with open weights.
content_en:
As decision models spread across the industry, a company called Musubi has a new idea for how to put them to work: moderating content. On Tuesday, Musubi announced a lightweight decision model made for real-time moderation called PolicyLM-1.7B, released with open weights.
The idea is to take a content policy written in plain English and apply it to messages in under 50 milliseconds. Musubi’s model is designed to be similar in cost and speed to the AI classifier systems that power moderation on most social platforms — but because it has the flexibility of a modern LLM, it can apply complex policies without special training. Even more important, the model won’t need new training when the policy changes, allowing for human policy-setters to iterate as much as they need.
As Musubi co-founder and chief AI officer Filip Jankovic sees it, it gives platform managers a way to label content proactively.
“Product teams just want a better understanding of what’s happening on their platform, especially as the amount of content is exponentially increasing,” Jankovic says. “Being able to label all of that in a very scalable, customizable way is extremely useful.”
Decision models have become a hot topic in the AI world since the release of TypeSafe AI’s Jev in September, which was shortly followed by competing decision models from OpenAI and Amazon. Instead of outputting text, a decision model outputs outcome probabilities, though in this case the model outputs a binary judgement: Either the content is in the category or it isn’t. By limiting the model’s output to a set of predetermined choices, decision models are able to run faster and cheaper than large language models, while still maintaining the flexibility of the transformer architecture.
One early use case is reining in misbehavior by AI agents — so it’s only natural to apply the same technology to human misbehavior.
Notably, Jankovic says his interest in decision models predates Jev, tracing it back to a 2024 project called GLiNER (Generalist Model for Named Entity Recognition) that deployed many of the same techniques.
Still, Musubi isn’t wary of the comparison. If anything, the company is eager to use the new interest in decision models to shine a light on content moderation. “If Jev caught your eye, PolicyLM-1.7B is the same kind of model, trained specifically for content moderation, that you can run yourself,” the product announcement reads.

title_en: Google’s power-hungry data centers crave nuclear energy
title_fa: Google’s power-hungry data centers crave nuclear energy
excerpt_en: Google announced a new agreement to update six nuclear power plant sites across the US as the tech giant seeks to generate more electricity for its power-hungry data centers. Google signed the 20-year deal with Constellation, the leading nuclear power plant operator in the US....
excerpt_fa: Google announced a new agreement to update six nuclear power plant sites across the US as the tech giant seeks to generate more electricity for its power-hungry data centers. Google signed the 20-year deal with Constellation, the leading nuclear power plant operator in the US....
content_en:
Google announced a new agreement to update six nuclear power plant sites across the US as the tech giant seeks to generate more electricity for its power-hungry data centers.
Google’s power-hungry data centers crave nuclear energy
Google signed long-term agreements meant to cover the costs of upgrades at nuclear power plants.
Google signed long-term agreements meant to cover the costs of upgrades at nuclear power plants.
Google signed the 20-year deal with Constellation, the leading nuclear power plant operator in the US. The power purchase agreement is meant to guarantee the revenue needed to cover the cost of efficiency upgrades at existing nuclear plants and “represents more than $4.3 billion of new investment by Constellation,” according to the press release.
Over the next five years, the companies expect new equipment at each site to collectively lead to 890 megawatts of additional nuclear capacity. That’s roughly equivalent to the amount of electricity one large new nuclear reactor or three small modular reactors might generate, according to Google and Constellation.
PJM has struggled lately to meet growing demand from AI data centers
They plan to modernize 11 reactors at six sites in Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. Each is connected to the PJM Interconnection grid, the largest power grid in the US, which spans 13 states and the District of Columbia — including the nation’s largest hub for data centers in Loudoun County, Virginia.
PJM has struggled lately to meet growing demand from AI data centers. An independent market monitor filed a complaint last year with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) saying that PJM was planning to allow huge data centers to connect to the grid that it could not reliably serve, which could lead to blackouts.
In January, the Trump administration and governors from all of the states where PJM operates issued a joint statement calling on PJM to hold an “emergency” power auction to support the buildout of new power plants through long-term contracts. PJM postponed its auction last week following a directive from FERC to revise its proposal in order to ensure stronger protections to prevent data centers from raising electricity bills for other customers. Electricity rates have skyrocketed in states connected to PJM, including New Jersey, where prices have climbed 54 percent over five years.
Along with the nuclear power deal, Google also inked a separate, much larger 15-year energy supply agreement with Constellation meant to guarantee continued revenue for other existing power plants Constellation operates within PJM, regardless of fuel type. Nuclear energy made up 70 percent of Constellation’s total generating capacity last year, and another 8 percent came from renewables. Gas and oil made up the remaining 22 percent, according to the company’s latest sustainability report. Gas also accounts for the largest chunk of PJM’s fuel mix. At 2,700MW, the second deal is much larger than the nuclear power purchase agreement.
Data centers are driving a surge in new gas infrastructure projects in the US, moving many tech companies further from their sustainability goals. Google’s carbon emissions rose by 18 percent last year along with a jump in electricity demand of 37 percent, according to the company’s latest sustainability report.

title_en: AI computing startup Lambda to raise $4B ahead of planned IPO
title_fa: AI computing startup Lambda to raise $4B ahead of planned IPO
excerpt_en: Nvidia-backed Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre-money valuation ahead of a planned 2027 IPO, led by Coatue and Blackstone.
excerpt_fa: Nvidia-backed Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre-money valuation ahead of a planned 2027 IPO, led by Coatue and Blackstone.
content_en:
Cloud provider Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre-money valuation, marking what could be its last private round before a planned 2027 IPO, according to The Wall Street Journal. Coatue Management and Blackstone are leading the round.
A letter to investors reviewed by the Journal shows Lambda’s backlog grew from $15 billion in June to $50 billion in September. While that might look like a hearty increase in demand, much of that increase appears to be driven by a $35 billion commitment from one company: Anthropic, which signed a deal with Lambda in late August.
That means Lambda’s valuation, which has climbed significantly since its 2025 funding round, could be leaning heavily on Anthropic’s ability to keep paying. Still, with reliable GPU capacity so scarce, investors are clearly still willing to bet on companies that provide it, especially ones with large contracts with a major AI lab.
For neoclouds like Lambda, demand isn’t so much the problem as is the cost of meeting it. Data center buildouts are largely funded by debt — of which Lambda just raised an additional $1 billion last week — and lenders are getting choosier about who they offer cash to and under what circumstances. Lambda’s decision to raise more now not only sets the tone for its IPO pricing, but also gives it access to more capital before the scrutiny of public markets arrives.
If and when Lambda does IPO — the company was reportedly meant to debut this year, but has pushed that back amid market uncertainty — it will join other Nvidia-backed neoclouds, like CoreWeave and Nebius, that now depend on the health of their stock to fund their data center buildouts. British neocloud Nscale filed for an IPO last month and is expected to begin trading soon.
Lambda, Coatue, and Blackstone did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

content_en:
Calling something “last-gen” usually means it comes with big compromises compared to the latest version. That’s not as true for the last-gen Kindle Paperwhite as it is with some other tech. The newer version can open books 30 percent faster (not the same as page-turning speed), and its aluminum design is a millimeter thinner — but it costs $50 more.
Amazon’s last-gen Kindle Paperwhite is 30 percent off
$170 gets you the Signature Edition without ads, plus 32GB of storage and wireless charging.
$170 gets you the Signature Edition without ads, plus 32GB of storage and wireless charging.
The 2024 edition has the same fantastic 300ppi screen, an auto-adjusting front light, and waterproof (IPX8) design. And the Signature Edition that’s discounted has no lockscreen ads, twice the storage (32GB) of the base model, plus wireless charging and an ambient light sensor, and it’s down to $169.99 (originally $249.99) at Amazon.
Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition
The premium Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition offers the same design and performance as the standard model but with more storage and support for wireless charging.
The standard Paperwhite is $149.99 (was $199.99) at Amazon, and while the lower price is nice, I’d suggest only opting for that model if you’re alright with what you’re giving up (which is a lot): it has half the storage, no wireless charging, and lockscreen ads.

title_en: The next hurdle for AI agents: getting websites to let them in
title_fa: The next hurdle for AI agents: getting websites to let them in
excerpt_en: Personal AI agents promise to shop, book flights, and make reservations for you. But deliberate blocks and anti-bot defenses are getting in the way, leaving consumers caught in the middle. A new standard aims to help.
excerpt_fa: Personal AI agents promise to shop, book flights, and make reservations for you. But deliberate blocks and anti-bot defenses are getting in the way, leaving consumers caught in the middle. A new standard aims to help.
content_en:
Personal AI agents, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, ChatGPT’s Dots, and others, are kicking off a new wave of consumer AI that involves more than just responding to queries. These AI agents can actually get things done on users’ behalf, like booking flights, making dinner reservations, ordering groceries, and more, all without having to be technical enough to set up OpenClaw or some other agent on your own computer.
But consumers adopting these agents are often running into issues when the website on the other end of their request blocks the AI from completing the job.
Most recently, Amazon began blocking Meta’s Muse AI agent from its retail site, meaning that the agent could no longer browse or make purchases from its product catalog.
However, the problem is not limited to Amazon or Muse. User complaints across social media indicate their agents are often running into similar blocks. Some of these are intentional, like Amazon’s, while others are the result of websites’ traditional anti-bot measures designed to protect against spam and malicious activity.
What’s not clear to the end user is whether or not the block is accidental on the website owner’s part, which leaves them frustrated with both the service provider or retailer and the agent trying to facilitate the transaction.
For instance, TechCrunch has seen a handful of complaints on social media claiming that Muse couldn’t complete a purchase on Walmart’s retail website. (NBC also reported that this was a problem Walmart had faced in its tests of the AI agent.)
But a spokesperson for Walmart told us these weren’t intentional. In fact, Walmart is partnered with Muse, as was announced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September. The company said it wants to be where its customers are, and that now includes being available through AI agent experiences.
The issue that Walmart customers often appear to be running into (see below) is that the website presents a button that has to be clicked to verify the visitor is human. If that experience is interrupted, the check could fail, and the agent gets booted out.
It’s an indication that the current technology we use to verify humans and keep websites safe from spam and bots may not be the best fit for the agent-first era of the web we’re now moving into.
To address this problem, industry partners including Meta, Walmart, Stripe, Sierra, Genesys, Rocket, NiCE, and Decagon have begun working on an open standard that would dictate how AI agents can communicate with businesses, helping to separate the good bots acting on behalf of the user and the bad. This protocol will be specifically focused on agent-to-agent communication for the purposes of online commerce, Meta said in a blog post.
In the meantime, consumer confusion abounds.
Although Walmart is at least trying to be accessible via AI agents, other companies aren’t so keen on the idea or haven’t fully embraced the technology.
For example, flight booking is currently one of the main use cases being positioned for agents, but many people have reported issues with airlines rejecting their agents’ requests.
Delta, for instance, told us that the company is taking steps to protect customers from unauthorized automated activity, and that if it were to open up to AI agents, it would have to be done with “security and the customer experience in mind.”
“While Delta does not currently have a partnership or integration that enables a third-party AI agent to shop for or book Delta flights on a customer’s behalf on our digital platforms, we’re continuing to evaluate how new technology, including external AI agents, could enhance the way customers engage with Delta,” said Delta’s general manager of Global Communications, Heena Chavda, in response to our questions about whether or not it was blocking agents, as some users complained.
United was not quite as direct as Delta, but a spokesperson pointed us to the part of its Terms of Use policy, which says that the user agrees “not to use any robot, spider, other automatic device, or manual process to monitor or copy this website or the content contained therein or for any other unauthorized purpose without United’s prior written permission.” (United didn’t respond to a follow-up question about whether it was blocking specific personal AI agents, like Muse.)
Early adopters’ complaints across social media have referenced a number of brands that are reportedly blocking AI agents, including Yelp, eBay, Zillow, Pizza Hut, Adidas, and various airlines. Some believe that the blocking activity seems to have recently increased.
A couple of people even said eBay suspended their accounts because of their use of agentic AI. Another complained that Google kicked out Instinct while it was cleaning up their Gmail inbox for them.
Despite the push to have agents book tables at restaurants and other tedious tasks, Yelp told us that it doesn’t permit non-human traffic on its platform unless the agent has paid to access Yelp’s content and data through its data licensing program. That means agents trying to use its site to get a quote, add a user to a waitlist, or book them a table will likely fail if they don’t have a formal partnership with Yelp.
eBay told TechCrunch that its approach is not to prohibit all third-party shopping agents from completing purchases. Instead, its policies restrict unauthorized agents and actions, like automated scraping and model training.
Adidas, Zillow, and Pizza Hut either didn’t respond or declined to provide a comment by the time of publication.
One major company involved in this space is Cloudflare, which offers sites protection from AI agents that could be training on its data and managing other automated activity. Some of these are intentional, like Amazon’s, while others are the result of websites’ traditional anti-bot measures designed to protect against spam and malicious activity.
What’s not clear to the end user is whether or not the block is accidental on the website owner’s part, which leaves them frustrated with both the service provider or retailer and the agent trying to facilitate the transaction.
For instance, TechCrunch has seen a handful of complaints on social media claiming that Muse couldn’t complete a purchase on Walmart’s retail website. (NBC also reported that this was a problem Walmart had faced in its tests of the AI agent.)
But a spokesperson for Walmart told us these weren’t intentional. In fact, Walmart is partnered with Muse, as was announced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September. The company said it wants to be where its customers are, and that now includes being available through AI agent experiences.
The issue that Walmart customers often appear to be running into (see below) is that the website presents a button that has to be clicked to verify the visitor is human. If that experience is interrupted, the check could fail, and the agent gets booted out.
It’s an indication that the current technology we use to verify humans and keep websites safe from spam and bots may not be the best fit for the agent-first era of the web we’re now moving into.
To address this problem, industry partners including Meta, Walmart, Stripe, Sierra, Genesys, Rocket, NiCE, and Decagon have begun working on an open standard that would dictate how AI agents can communicate with businesses, helping to separate the good bots acting on behalf of the user and the bad. This protocol will be specifically focused on agent-to-agent communication for the purposes of online commerce, Meta said in a blog post.
In the meantime, consumer confusion abounds.
Although Walmart is at least trying to be accessible via AI agents, other companies aren’t so keen on the idea or haven’t fully embraced the technology.
For example, flight booking is currently one of the main use cases being positioned for agents, but many people have reported issues with airlines rejecting their agents’ requests.
Delta, for instance, told us that the company is taking steps to protect customers from unauthorized automated activity, and that if it were to open up to AI agents, it would have to be done with “security and the customer experience in mind.”
“While Delta does not currently have a partnership or integration that enables a third-party AI agent to shop for or book Delta flights on a customer’s behalf on our digital platforms, we’re continuing to evaluate how new technology, including external AI agents, could enhance the way customers engage with Delta,” said Delta’s general manager of Global Communications, Heena Chavda, in response to our questions about whether or not it was blocking agents, as some users complained.
United was not quite as direct as Delta, but a spokesperson pointed us to the part of its Terms of Use policy, which says that the user agrees “not to use any robot, spider, other automatic device, or manual process to monitor or copy this website or the content contained therein or for any other unauthorized purpose without United’s prior written permission.” (United didn’t respond to a follow-up question about whether it was blocking specific personal AI agents, like Muse.)
Early adopters’ complaints across social media have referenced a number of brands that are reportedly blocking AI agents, including Yelp, eBay, Zillow, Pizza Hut, Adidas, and various airlines. Some believe that the blocking activity seems to have recently increased.
A couple of people even said eBay suspended their accounts because of their use of agentic AI. Another complained that Google kicked out Instinct while it was cleaning up their Gmail inbox for them.
Despite the push to have agents book tables at restaurants and other tedious tasks, Yelp told us that it doesn’t permit non-human traffic on its platform unless the agent has paid to access Yelp’s content and data through its data licensing program. That means agents trying to use its site to get a quote, add a user to a waitlist, or book them a table will likely fail if they don’t have a formal partnership with Yelp.
eBay told TechCrunch that its approach is not to prohibit all third-party shopping agents from completing purchases. Instead, its policies restrict unauthorized agents and actions, like automated scraping and model training.
Adidas, Zillow, and Pizza Hut either didn’t respond or declined to provide a comment by the time of publication.
One major company involved in this space is Cloudflare, which offers sites protection from AI agents that could be training on its data and managing other automated activity. Some suspect that Cloudflare and other content delivery networks (CDNs) like it are currently disrupting Muse traffic. This is attributed to a change to crawler defaults on September 15, which allows site owners to block AI training while allowing other types of bots. Existing...

content_en:
Amazon’s October Big Deal Days are underway (lasting through tomorrow night), and we spotted a ton of Apple products and accessories in the sale, ranging from laptops and headphones to desktops and more. Some of the deals are only for Prime members, but other retailers are often matching or beating Amazon’s prices, and we’ll continue to update our coverage as we spot those deals.
Save on MacBooks, iPads and Apple Watches during October Prime Day
Prime Big Deal Days is a great chance to save cash on the latest Apple tech.
Prime Big Deal Days is a great chance to save cash on the latest Apple tech.
If your sights are set beyond what Apple makes, our main roundup has over 100 of the best deals from October Prime Day, and we’re keeping it updated throughout the sale.
iPhone Air
The iPhone Air is Apple’s thinnest iPhone yet at 5.6mm, featuring a 6.5-inch ProMotion display, a 48MP fusion camera, and an 18MP front camera with Center Stage support. But its single rear camera and “meh” battery life mean it’s not for everyone.
iPhone 16E
The iPhone 16E is the spiritual successor to the iPhone SE, bringing flagship-level performance for less than the standard 16. We really wish it included MagSafe for $599, but those upgrading from older iPhones will probably be satisfied with what’s included.
Apple AirPods Max (second-gen)
Apple’s second-generation AirPods Max have excellent sound and ANC performance, but are only a minor upgrade from the older pair. Read our review.
Apple 13-inch MacBook Air (M5)
Powered by Apple’s new M5 chip, the latest MacBook Airs are more powerful than prior models and offer double the base storage (512GB). They also support faster wireless standards, specifically Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Read our review.
Apple MacBook Air (15-inch, M5, 2026)
The 15-inch Apple MacBook Air features improved performance and better connectivity than the previous generation, and better speakers than the 13-inch model.
iPad Mini (2024)
The seventh-gen iPad Mini comes with Apple’s A17 Pro chip and support for Apple Intelligence. It’s also compatible with the Apple Pencil Pro and offers faster Wi-Fi and USB-C speeds. Read our review.
Belkin MagSafe 15W 2-in-1 wireless charging dock
A slick 2-in-1 charger that can charge your magnet-friendly iPhone or Pixel at a relatively speedy pace. Its extra charging pad supports AirPods, the Apple Watch, and other Qi-ready accessories.
Belkin Qi2.2 25W 2-in-1 foldable charging dock
Slap a recent iPhone onto this charging pad and it’ll charge at fast 25W speeds. It can also charge AirPods, and includes a cord and wall adapter.
Apple Watch SE 3
The Apple Watch SE 3 is a major glow-up, adding an always-on display, wrist-temperature sensor, a more powerful processor, and fast charging. Read our review.
AirPods Pro 3
The AirPods Pro 3 have a new design that improves their fit, superior noise cancellation, better bass, and fairly accurate heart rate sensors. Read our review.
Apple iPad Air M4
The M4-powered iPad Air excels at AI-powered tasks, and has great battery life, but the 60Hz screen feels underwhelming. Read our review.
iPad (2025)
Apple’s entry-level iPad is an excellent tablet for casual use, even if it is getting a little long in the tooth. Its high-res screen is great for watching video, and its A16 processor is still fast enough to handle light games and productivity apps. Read our review.
M6 Mac Mini
Apple’s recently-updated Mac Mini packs surprising performance into a small package, and the discount helps offset a generational price bump. Read our review.
Apple Watch Series 12
The newest generation of Apple Watch packs in a variety of upgrades, like faster charging and updated sensors, alongside new Siri and AI features. Read our review.
AirPods 4
Apple’s AirPods 4 are last-gen wireless earbuds, but they’re still great. The hard, plastic buds feature improved audio over the third-gen model, along with deep iOS integration and spatial audio with head tracking. Read our review.
Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max TechWoven Case with MagSafe
This Apple iPhone case features a woven fabric made from recycled polyester for a unique look and rugged protection.
Apple Pencil Pro
The Apple Pencil Pro arrives with new features like Find My support so you can find the stylus when it gets lost, as well as new creative capabilities like squeeze gestures and the “Barrel Roll” gyroscope.
Apple Magic Keyboard Folio for iPad (A16)
This keyboard for the iPad turns your tablet into a tiny laptop, and is detachable in case you’d rather just use the kickstand folio cover.
Speck Presidio2 Grip Case with MagSafe for Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone 17 Pro Max
This Speck case features specially designed grips that help prevent accidental drops, and is made from 50 percent recycled plastic.
The Force Case from Casetify comes in a handful of trendy colors, and supports MagSafe accessories and chargers.

title_en: Doom on the Vectrex turns the classic shooter into Tron-like vector art
title_fa: Doom on the Vectrex turns the classic shooter into Tron-like vector art
excerpt_en: With some processing caveats of course.
excerpt_fa: With some processing caveats of course.
content_en:
Doom on the Vectrex turns the classic shooter into Tron-like vector art
The 1993 game runs on the 1982 console thanks to a modded cartridge.
Vector graphics were mostly abandoned in gaming, but small pockets of enthusiasts are still keeping the Vectrex, the only vector-based home console ever released, alive. And what does one do to draw attention to a niche platform? Why, put Doom on it, of course.
We've seen Doom find a home on an odd array of devices, including iPods, graphing calculators and toasters. Unlike many other strange Doom ports, though, the Vectrex version (via Time Extension) offers a truly unique visual language. That comes from the console's fundamentally different display: instead of a grid of pixels, it steers an electron beam to trace lines on the screen directly. This gives the game its Tron-like appearance, with clean lines that make it seem more like an artistic statement than just another silly port.
How does a console that predates Doom by 11 years run the game? Well, it technically doesn't. Modder Jason Kopp (ArcadeJason) built the demo around his Ultimate Vectrex Multicart 2 (UVMC2), a cartridge that essentially acts as a small plug-in PC. The UVMC2 handles the processing while using the console's built-in CRT for the display. Meanwhile, audio comes through the cartridge's separate 3.5mm output. The project also uses an SDK created by modder Daniel Ferrer Guerrero.
Even with the asterisk that this isn't a native Vectrex port, the result is still one of the more notable Doom visual presentations we've seen. You can check out Kopp's work below.

title_en: Skydance will combine HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single streaming service
title_fa: Skydance will combine HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single streaming service
excerpt_en: Please don't name it ParaMax.
excerpt_fa: Please don't name it ParaMax.
content_en:
Skydance will combine HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single streaming service
The newly merged media company plans to 'unify' its new streaming businesses.
Skydance, the new media entity made from Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, is also going to merge its streaming apps. The company shared its intentions in the same announcement that confirmed the $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. was complete, a nearly year's long process that was briefly blocked by a multi-state lawsuit until Paramount reached a settlement in late September.
While Skydance didn't get into specifics, it did share that its streaming services, which now include HBO Max, Paramount+ and Discovery+, "will unify into a single service over time." Plans to combine the streaming services have been on the table for a while. In March, Variety reported Skydance CEO David Ellison intended to combine Paramount+ and HBO Max into a single entity, giving the company "a little over 200 million direct-to-consumer subscribers." Ellison also stressed that HBO would continue to "operate with independence" after the merger. Based on Skydance's recent appointment of HBO CEO Casey Bloys to Co-Chair and Chief Content Officer of Skydance DTC, the company is hoping some of that prestige HBO quality can rub off on its other programming.
Reducing redundancies and combining catalogues of content is what all entertainment companies do after merging. HBO Max is a recent example: Since it launched as Max in 2023, the service has offered Discovery's catalog of reality TV and documentary programming alongside WarnerMedia's collection of movies and TV series.
That same merger process typically results in some negative outcomes too, like layoffs — which Skydance has already warned employees about — and higher prices. Skydance hasn't announced the name of its unified streaming service, let alone what it'll cost, but given the exorbitant amount of debt the company took on as part of the merger, there's a good chance it could be higher than what customers paid before.

title_en: Google Photos vs. Gallery app: What's the difference and which should you use?
title_fa: Google Photos vs. Gallery app: What's the difference and which should you use?
excerpt_en: We compare Google's Photos and Gallery apps, so you can decide which one to use.
excerpt_fa: We compare Google's Photos and Gallery apps, so you can decide which one to use.
content_en:
Google Photos vs. Gallery app: What's the difference and which should you use?
Gallery is a pared-down option if you don’t need Photos’ cloud backup and editing features.
Did you know that Google has another, simpler app for images called Gallery? We're not talking about preloaded applications made by Android brands like Samsung's Gallery, but an app that Google itself developed. It's a stripped-down alternative you can use if you don't really care for most of Google Photos' features and just want something that will let you organize your images.
If you're wondering which one you should use between the two, well... you don't really have to pick. You may have to download the Gallery app from Google Play, but you can have both on your phone and just use one or the other when you want to.
Photos has cloud backup, Gallery doesn't
One of the most important differences between the two apps is that Photos can automatically back up your images to the cloud, whereas Gallery can't. You can switch on automatic backup in Photos by tapping on your avatar at the top right corner of the screen and then Backup, where you can toggle on the option.
You can see how much cloud storage space you can free up on your profile, as well. Old personal Google accounts come with 15GB of free storage, but new accounts created on or after March 9, 2026 only come with 5GB by default, with the option to unlock 10GB more by verifying a valid phone number. Your storage is shared across the Google services you use, including Gmail, Drive, WhatsApp and, yes, Photos. To expand your storage space, you will have to pay for a Google One subscription, which will cost you $2 per month for 100GB of storage or $3 for 200GB.
Buying additional storage is probably the quickest way to make sure you don't run out of space on your phone. You'll also see the option Free up space on this device when you tap on your profile image within the Photos app. Doing that will delete items from your device that are already safely backed up to the cloud in the quality of your choice. One important thing to keep in mind is that if you manually move images to Trash in both Photos and Gallery, they will also be permanently removed from your cloud backup and all the devices where you have the app installed after 30 days.
If you don't mind regularly and manually backing up your device, as well as deleting images from your phone, you can simply use the Gallery app. You can buy an external storage drive that plugs into your phone's USB-C port to save your photos instead of relying on cloud backup.
Photos has more comprehensive editing tools than Gallery
Since Gallery is a simpler app, it also has minimal editing tools. It has Rotate, Crop and a handful of filters you can apply to your images. Meanwhile, Google Photos has access to a wider range of editing tools, including AI enhancements. You'll be able to adjust an image's brightness, contrast, tone, highlights and shadows in Photos. You can add blurring effects, sharpen and even move certain elements to other parts of the image. You can also doodle on the image, add text and highlights and use a one-tap tool that automatically smoothens skin texture, whitens teen and reduces under-eye shadows.
If you regularly edit your images, Photos may be the better app for you, unless you already have a trusty editing app. Gallery is good enough if you just want to crop your photos sometimes. You can share images to social media or send them via email or messagings app through both Google Photos and Gallery anyway, so that doesn't have to factor into your choice.

title_en: Hark releases an AI personal assistant with a focus on privacy
title_fa: Hark releases an AI personal assistant with a focus on privacy
excerpt_en: The AI lab's personal assistant is an operating system from the future designed to compete with Muse, Dots, and Instinct.
excerpt_fa: The AI lab's personal assistant is an operating system from the future designed to compete with Muse, Dots, and Instinct.
content_en:
From Muse to Instinct to Dots, tech firms are hunting for the user experience that will make an AI personal assistant a must-have product.
Hark, a startup founded less than a year ago by serial founder Brett Adcock, is throwing its hat in the ring today with the wide release of Hark Pro. Users can access the service for free, with a subscription tier for heavy users.
The company sees its mission as building a user interface for AI, not creating AGI or curing cancer. The foundation is a model trained specifically for computer use, and that’s what Hark Pro does — it uses your computer for you.
That’s perhaps a less ambitious claim than some frontier labs are making, but a little humility goes a long way in winning over users. And rather than an app, Hark’s goal is to create an operating system for the AI computers of our future.
Hark Pro is a full-screen experience with a kind of homepage, featuring a central chat dialog and a feed populated by prompts for actions you might need it to take and visualizations the company calls “panels” that offer mini-dashboards for things you’re interested in. The background is a piece of custom imagery tailored to the weather and time where you are.
Like other AI assistants, users configure it to access their digital life — email, calendar, hard drive, credit cards, etc. Then, it can take on digital tasks as well as fielding classic chatbot questions.
Abidur Chowdhury, a former Apple staffer who leads design at Hark, demoed the product for me. It proactively asked him about expenses he needed to approve, emails he needed to respond to, a meeting with this reporter, and, of course, pointed out that he needed to book a flight for a trip and offered to take care of it. (“I know the flight thing is put to death,” he admits, grinning.)
That does get at the challenge with these apps: One of the harder things for users is actually coming up with useful tasks they are capable of accomplishing. Chowdhury says he was impressed when the AI assistant recently recognized that one of his colleagues needed to renew their car registration at the California DMV, and handled it through the agency’s website.
One notable UX choice that Hark makes is showing the user how the agent navigates the web in a small window, an action most AI assistants perform without it surfacing in the app, which Chowdhury says is intended to build trust with users that the agent is doing the right thing.
That matters because part of Hark’s pitch is that they are not Meta or OpenAI — “we’re not here to like sell you ads and steal your data,” Chowdhury says. To truly leverage these models, users will need to share their entire digital lives. Beyond very real cybersecurity concerns, will users be comfortable with a company like Meta having its products create detailed profiles of their friends and family?
Asked about that kind of profiling, Chowdhury says that “we are doing work to understand you, and be helpful for what you need, but it’s really like task-related — it’s really about how Hark can help take something off your plate and be useful.”
What sets Hark Pro apart from its competitors, Chowdhury says, is its effort to fully subsitute for your computer, but also his belief that it just works better.

title_en: Asos hit by extortion hack that may have compromised some customer data
title_fa: Asos hit by extortion hack that may have compromised some customer data
excerpt_en: The attackers sent a push notification to Asos shoppers announcing their activity.
excerpt_fa: The attackers sent a push notification to Asos shoppers announcing their activity.
content_en:
Asos hit by extortion hack that may have compromised some customer data
The attackers sent a push notification to Asos shoppers announcing their activity.
UK-based fashion retailer Asos is doing damage control after its customers were sent a push notification claiming that its cloud services had been hacked. According to The Guardian, Asos users received mobile alerts that were addressed to the company's data protection officer and IT personnel.
The notifications read: "Dear Asos DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us or we will leak it." Snowflake is a cloud service that handles push notifications as well as managing data about transactions and customer demographics. A link in the message sent users to a Telegram channel claiming to be operated by Xuanye Group, a reportedly unknown name among most cybersecurity circles.
According to the company's statement, "We are investigating unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms that we use to communicate with customers. We took immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms and are working with our internal and external specialist advisers, as well as all relevant authorities."
Asos said that although customers' names and contact information may have been accessed in the hack, it did not believe payment details or passwords had been compromised. The company added that its app and website were operating as usual.

title_en: Why it's important to regularly replace your surge protectors
title_fa: Why it's important to regularly replace your surge protectors
excerpt_en: Time and spikes take a toll on a surge protector, even with no visible signs of damage.
excerpt_fa: Time and spikes take a toll on a surge protector, even with no visible signs of damage.
content_en:
Why it's important to regularly replace your surge protectors
Time and spikes take a toll on a surge protector, even with no visible signs of damage.
Few things in modern life are as convenient as a good surge protector. That small, narrow strip can literally protect thousands of dollars' worth of equipment, especially if you have a PC gaming setup or extensive home office equipment. Most basic plug-in surge protectors use components called metal-oxide varistors (MOVs), a fancy term for components that take the brunt of excess voltage and redirect it. Unfortunately, MOVs degrade over time, with or without voltage surges, and repeated spikes expedite an MOV surge protector's life cycle.
The wear and tear isn't exactly obvious either. Even if the surge protector successfully mitigates two or three surges, it will usually look like the same old boring plug-in strip. In fact, depending on the design, a surge protector will go right on powering your devices even though its internal MOV components are no longer working properly. Some will go the extra mile and shut off outlets when the protection mechanism fails.
It's worth adding that some surge protector designs use TVS diodes, silicon avalanche diodes (SADs) or gas discharge tube components. MOV is the most relevant example here because it's the most common in households by far, and there is a narrow set of use cases for TVS diodes, SADs, and GDTs.
Check the light, not just the outlets
First and foremost, you need to determine if you're actually using a surge protector or just a power strip, since the two look nearly identical. On a surge protector, there's usually an indicator labeled "Protected" or "Protection Present," something along those lines. If you see that label, consult your instructions for that particular model. On some, an unlit protection indicator means the surge-suppression components have failed. Keeping those instructions handy or Googling the model will tell you what means what and why.
Discard and replace the surge protector if the instructions tell you the light indicates protection has failed. Obviously, if your surge protector is smoking, scorch marks are present or the plastic is melting, it's time to ditch it for a new one. It kind of goes without saying that if a lightning bolt strikes your backyard, squirrels are falling out of trees and you have to peel the housecat off your face, replace the surge protector after the storm clears.
Also, avoid plugging things like space heaters into surge protector strips because a strip can overheat under that kind of load, or degrade much faster than normal.
Is five years a good deadline?
Not necessarily, at least not for every surge protector. How long one lasts depends on its design and the number and/or size of the surges it's dealt with. Some manufacturers suggest considering replacement every three to five years, especially since you can rarely keep count of how many surges it's handled over time. However, that's a suggestion and nothing more. It's far from a guarantee that even an exceptional, premium surge protector will last up to five years.
If you have no idea how old the strip is and can't tell if it's still providing protection, replacing it is the smartest avenue. Anytime a surge protector is replaced, look for clear protection status indicators and mark down the purchase date somewhere practical. Last but not least, don't pretend that a surge protector is an all-out lightning shield. This isn't a Marvel movie, and no standard surge protection device can handle a direct lightning strike.
The thing about surge protectors is that they're all a bit different. Some use lights, while others trip a simple switch like a breaker box. Some lights mean different things. The best route is to learn about what you're purchasing, how it functions and replace it when the instructions say. Don't trust it to last five years, especially if you live in an area where afternoon thunderstorms are common.

title_en: India’s JioHotstar takes partnership route for Middle East expansion
title_fa: India’s JioHotstar takes partnership route for Middle East expansion
excerpt_en: JioHotstar will be offered inside Starzplay rather than through a stand-alone service.
excerpt_fa: JioHotstar will be offered inside Starzplay rather than through a stand-alone service.
content_en:
JioHotstar, the streaming platform with more than 500 million monthly active users backed by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries, is expanding into the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) through Starzplay, one of the region’s largest streaming services. The new overseas push comes after its debut in the U.K., Canada, and Singapore.
Under the partnership announced Tuesday, JioHotstar will have a dedicated section in Starzplay’s app and on its website, offering Indian films, TV shows, originals, and reality franchises across multiple languages. This is different from JioHotstar’s September launch in the U.K., Canada, and Singapore, where it replaced Hotstar and debuted as a stand-alone streaming service.
The expansion is part of Reliance’s push to build JioHotstar into a global streaming platform after establishing a massive audience in India. MENA has one of the world’s largest South Asian diaspora communities, giving JioHotstar a sizable potential audience for its Indian films, television shows, and original programming.
As with its earlier debut in the U.K., Canada, and Singapore, JioHotstar’s own sports offering in India will not be available in MENA. However, a plan bundling JioHotstar with Starzplay’s sports offering, including cricket, is priced at AED 49.99 (about $13.60) a month. JioHotstar is also available through Starzplay’s Plus monthly plan at AED 34.99 (around $9.50).
With MENA’s large Indian diaspora in focus, new JioHotstar originals will premiere in the region simultaneously with their release in India, with audio available in up to 10 languages. The catalog spans Hindi, Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu, and Bangla, among other languages, and includes shows such as “Bigg Boss” and “Koffee with Karan.” Additionally, JioHotstar is putting particular emphasis on Malayalam programming, given the large Malayali population in the region.
JioHotstar was created after Reliance and Disney merged their Indian media businesses into an $8.5 billion joint venture in 2024. The service, which combined JioCinema and Disney+ Hotstar, launched in India in February last year.
Before JioHotstar’s launch, Hotstar was available in MENA. Disney Star expanded its distribution deal with evision, e&’s media and entertainment arm, in 2024, making it the regional home of Hotstar Specials. Evision is also a major shareholder in Starzplay, where JioHotstar will now have its first dedicated streaming presence in the region.
Starzplay counts more than 2.3 million subscribers and has built a sizable South Asian audience in part through its cricket offering.
Financial terms of the partnership were not disclosed. Starzplay CEO Maaz Sheikh described bringing JioHotstar to the platform as a “strategic investment.”

title_en: Don't throw away your old digital camera — do this instead
title_fa: Don't throw away your old digital camera — do this instead
excerpt_en: Your old camera might give video calls an upgrade, as long as USB support or clean HDMI keeps the setup sensible.
excerpt_fa: Your old camera might give video calls an upgrade, as long as USB support or clean HDMI keeps the setup sensible.
content_en:
Don't throw away your old digital camera — do this instead
Your old camera might give video calls an upgrade.
Old digital cameras are making a weird comeback, so it may feel a bit more difficult to justify throwing one in the electronics recycling bin than it would have a few years ago. According to the Camera & Imaging Products Association, shipments of built-in-lens digital cameras grew 29.6 percent in 2025 to approximately 2.44 million units, and are projected to increase an additional 13.6 percent in 2026. (CIPA didn't attribute that growth specifically to the current trend of retro digicams.)
If you already have one lying around, however, there's another reason to keep it. There are a lot of older DSLRs, mirrorless cameras and even some compact cameras that can be used as webcams. That can translate to improved low-light performance, greater control over framing or the natural background blur that laptop webcams devote a lot of software to trying to replicate. The trick is finding out whether yours can do it without turning a free upgrade into an expensive side project.
See if it works over USB first
Start with the specific model number and the manufacturer's webcam compatibility list. Canon's EOS 6D and EOS Rebel T6 are still supported, as are Nikon's D5300 and D750 with its Webcam Utility and Sony's A5100, A7 II and RX100 IV with Imaging Edge Webcam.
If your camera is listed, then setup can be rather simple. Install the manufacturer's webcam software if required, connect the camera using a USB data cable, put it into the appropriate video or remote mode and select it as the camera in Zoom, Google Meet or Microsoft Teams. You might already have everything you need.
However, a larger camera does not necessarily result in a clearer webcam picture. Some older supported Nikon DSLRs use only the VGA portion of Nikon's XGA live-view display, so a newer dedicated webcam might be able to capture more detail. Depending on the camera model, the camera can compensate for some of this ground with a larger sensor, better low-light performance and control over the lens.
Audio and power should be checked as well. Nikon and Sony say their webcam utilities don't send the camera's microphone audio to the computer, which means using your laptop mic or a separate microphone. If you're using live view for a long meeting, it will also drain the battery, so if the camera allows, external power might be worth setting up.
HDMI can work, but check the cost first
The experiment doesn't have to stop if there is no support for USB webcam. Cameras with clean HDMI output can be connected through a capture device, which then shows up as a webcam on your computer. "Clean" is the important word here. No one wants autofocus boxes, exposure settings and a flashing battery icon on the weekly Teams call.
Continuous operation matters as well. Elgato suggests checking if power saving can be turned off and if the camera can be powered externally while transmitting video. There are some older cameras that were not meant to be used as desk accessories for hours.
The issue is cost. Elgato's Cam Link 4K is priced at $99.99, excluding an HDMI cable, mount and/or possibly a dummy battery. Our current webcam guide, on the other hand, covers the 2K Anker PowerConf C200 at $60, which comes with microphones and a much simpler USB setup. Mac users might also be able to use a compatible iPhone, while Windows 11 users can use a compatible Android phone as a webcam for free.
Also consider the resale value of the camera before buying accessories. Some of the older digicams have been sold for much more than owners would expect because of the interest in them. According to B&H, one of its writers purchased a Canon PowerShot S95 for $130 in 2023, and it was selling for an average of over $400 in 2026.

title_en: Mirror Particle is building a ‘world model’ of human behavior
title_fa: Mirror Particle is building a ‘world model’ of human behavior
excerpt_en: Mirror Particle will launch at TechCrunch Disrupt's Startup Battlefield 200 with a world model built from scratch to predict human behavior, arguing that LLM role-play falls short for market research and brand strategy.
excerpt_fa: Mirror Particle will launch at TechCrunch Disrupt's Startup Battlefield 200 with a world model built from scratch to predict human behavior, arguing that LLM role-play falls short for market research and brand strategy.
content_en:
Startups that promise to predict how humans will behave are having a moment. Over the past year, Simile raised $200 million at a $2 billion valuation; Aaru raised $88 million at a $1 billion valuation; and Humans&, an AI startup that announced a massive $480 million seed round in January at a $4.48 billion valuation, launched Persimmon to model human behavior.
The status quo for human behavior prediction today relies heavily on large language models (LLMs) that are prompted or fine-tuned to role-play as a target demographic. But two-year-old, San Francisco-based Mirror Particle thinks that approach is fundamentally broken.
“It’s like bringing a super soaker to Niagara Falls,” says Abhivyakti Ahuja, co-founder and CEO of Mirror Particle, which provides brands with an AI engine that predicts consumer behavior and the reasons behind it. “LLMs have been trained on hundreds of billions of data points. How much can you influence its behavior by [fine-tuning] with such a small amount of data? It’s still stuck in the past.”
Ahuja doesn’t think LLMs see the world the way a human does. “LLMs are modeling written language, but humans are made of visual perception, spatial reasoning, social intelligence.” Relying on them, she says, means getting insights based on what humans don’t notice, which is beside the point when trying to predict human behavior.
Mirror Particle is taking another approach: building a foundation model, or as Ahuja describes it, a world model built from scratch that simulates why humans do what they do and how human behavior changes over time.
“We don’t want to capture the static person,” Ahuja said. “We want to capture the changing person. That means capturing the longitudinal data on how people are changing, what triggers are changing them and to what degree.” If they aren’t changing, she added, “that’s also a signal.”
Mirror Particle has already raised an angel round and says it’s close to closing its first venture round. The company is also competing next week in Startup Battlefield 200, TechCrunch’s renowned startup competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on October 13-15.
The startup relies on a proprietary combination of data that includes its clients’ customer data, current events, pop culture, social media, and more to model a demographic segment, thinking of it as a system that evolves over time and tracking how motivations shift as it moves through experiences. Much of the focus is on “revealed behavior” — what people actually do rather than self-reported survey answers.
Like its rivals, Mirror Particle’s initial go-to-market strategy focuses on where budgets already exist for these kinds of insights: market research and brand and product strategy. Mirror might, for instance, help a beauty brand not just write better ad copy for makeup that would appeal to Gen Z, but also determine if that demographic even wants that product.
“What if [the target demographic] doesn’t want eyeshadow palettes?” Ahuja said. “Maybe blush is a better option to go for if you want to sell a product to this market.”
Mirror Particle’s prediction engine also provides customers with the “why” behind current or future behavior — the motivations, constraints, and additional context that justify its recommendation, helping brands make smarter decisions.

title_en: Furientis lands $25M from Benchmark to mass-produce low-cost missile interceptors
title_fa: Furientis lands $25M from Benchmark to mass-produce low-cost missile interceptors
excerpt_en: The storied Silicon Valley firm makes its first pure defense investment.
excerpt_fa: The storied Silicon Valley firm makes its first pure defense investment.
content_en:
Until recently, venture capitalists largely steered clear of defense startups. Investments in the sector were viewed as morally controversial, and the process of securing government contracts was too lengthy and uncertain to justify venture funding.
But that sentiment changed rapidly after conflicts in Ukraine and Iran began to deplete the U.S. military’s missile supply. Startups that prove they can build equipment fast and affordably now stand a real chance of landing a Pentagon contract on an expedited timeline.
Four years into the defense tech boom that arguably began when Russia invaded Ukraine, the storied Silicon Valley venture firm Benchmark is placing its first bet on a pure defense startup.
Benchmark is leading a $25 million seed round into Furientis, a startup on a mission to mass-produce interceptor missiles. Just one year old, the company—whose name means “of fury” in Latin—has already secured a funded Pentagon contract to build mid-range interceptors. The startup was valued at $125 million, according to a person familiar with the company.
Furientis’ seed round follows a $5 million pre-seed that was announced in May.
“What they accomplished with just a pre-seed round was nothing short of remarkable,” Benchmark general partner Chetan Puttagunta, told TechCrunch. “They manufactured prototypes with just $5 million. They had they had already successfully done [a dozen] launches by the time we invested.”
That efficiency is in stark contrast to the slow-moving, high-cost development models used by traditional defense primes. The startup’s velocity is driven by its co-founders, who bring years of aerospace and defense engineering experience. Brody Franzen served as deputy chief engineer at Virgin Galactic before joining Castelion, a hypersonic missile startup valued at $13 billion, while Aris Simsarian previously led rocket engine testing at Virgin Orbit.
The duo launched Furientis after realizing the U.S. military is facing a severe shortage of “exquisite” missiles, which can cost around $3 million each, to counter inexpensive adversary threats, Franzen told TechCrunch.
According to Franzen, the U.S. Navy receives a mere 300 to 500 interceptor missiles annually, compared to China, which claims a production rate of 3,000 anti-ship cruise missiles a month.
“We’re being outproduced by a factor of 100 plus,” he said. “That is why we started the company.”
Furientis is not aiming to match the performance of best-in-class missile interceptors; instead, it is designing and manufacturing its systems so they can be assembled quickly from readily available components. As a result, each unit costs a fraction of legacy interceptors, a compelling value proposition for a Pentagon desperate to scale inventory within strict budget limits.
Unlike traditional defense primes such as Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, which are bogged down by long design cycles, Furientis has been testing its missiles in the field on a bi-weekly basis. The startup’s ultimate goal is to manufacture 1,000 systems a year in each factory. But for now, the young company is working out of its facility in Los Angeles, and taking its prototypes for trial launches to White Sands, New Mexico.
Given the need, Furientis is not the only company working on helping the government restock its stockpiles. Franzen said that larger defense startups like Anduril, Castelion, and Shield AI are also racing to build mass-produced interceptors, while traditional primes scramble to modernize their own manufacturing cycles.
Benchmark’s Puttagunta is not fazed by the seemingly crowded space. “I think there’s opportunity for lots more companies in this sector,” he said.

title_en: Learn all about scaling, fundraising, founder how-tos, and more at TechCrunch Founder Summit, November 4
title_fa: Learn all about scaling, fundraising, founder how-tos, and more at TechCrunch Founder Summit, November 4
excerpt_en: There isn’t a single manual to read or prompt to give an LLM that can equip you with the skills and knowledge to build a company. But on November 4, TechCrunch Founder Summit gives founders the next-best thing: A packed day at Boston's SoWa Power Station, where investors and...
excerpt_fa: There isn’t a single manual to read or prompt to give an LLM that can equip you with the skills and knowledge to build a company. But on November 4, TechCrunch Founder Summit gives founders the next-best thing: A packed day at Boston's SoWa Power Station, where investors and...
content_en:
There isn’t a single manual to read or prompt to give an LLM that can equip you with the skills and knowledge to build a company. But on November 4, TechCrunch Founder Summit gives founders the next-best thing: A packed day at Boston’s SoWa Power Station, where investors and operators share how they’ve navigated crucial decisions.
The Founder Summit’s agenda is built around core questions every founder eventually has to answer about capital, leadership, and what they’re actually building toward. And each session is designed to build upon each other. Like your startup’s founding team, these sessions work together to drive outcomes.
This is a breakdown on how the full event agenda fits together, and what you can expect to learn by attending. Keep in mind that tickets are at their lowest price point before they increase on October 16, so this is the ideal moment to grab your seat. You can save $200 on both Investor and Founder passes up until that deadline.
For a limited time, you can also get a second ticket for 50% off, and for even larger groups, there are bundle discounts available to groups of four or more.
Capital: How you raise, and who you raise from
Fundraising advice often stops at “How do I get the term sheet?” This track goes further, because getting a yes is only half of the equation. The other half is making sure it’s the right yes.
Underscore partner Brian Devaney opens with a candid read on today’s fundraising climate, including what investors are actually screening for right now, how founders can differentiate in a crowded market, and the specific moments where founders give up leverage without realizing it.
That’s the part most founders obsess over — as well as who ends up on the cap table once the round closes. This is where Vineet Edupuganti, co-founder and CEO of Cogent Security, picks up the thread. After raising an $11 million round, he learned firsthand that not every check is equal. He’ll walk through how to actually evaluate investors and navigate those trade-offs before you sign, not after.
This all frames fundraising as a two-part decision. First, win the leverage in the room, then spend it wisely on the right partners. Founders who only solve the first part often find themselves fighting their own cap table later.
Grab your pass and get all these fundraising insights. Bring your co-founder at 50% off.
Leadership: When the job changes, so does the team you need
No founder stays the same kind of leader forever. After all, the skills that get a company to its initial customers rarely match what’s needed when its customer list expands and the employee count grows. This track tackles that shift from two angles: the founder’s evolution, and the decisions on employees that either support or sabotage it.
HubSpot co-founder and Sequoia partner Brian Halligan has experienced this arc many times, first by building through HubSpot’s own stages of growth and now by advising founders doing the same from the investor’s seat. He’ll unpack how the CEO job transforms at each stage, the leadership habits that stop working once a company outgrows them, and how to keep reinventing yourself without losing what made you effective in the first place.
But a founder’s evolution doesn’t happen in isolation — it’s constrained by who’s actually in the building. NEA partner Melissa Taunton brings the hiring half of that equation, breaking down how early team decisions quietly set the ceiling on a company’s culture, speed, and ability to execute long before anyone notices the cracks. The founders who scale smoothly, in her experience, are the ones who treat early hires as architecture decisions, not just headcount.
Get your ticket, learn the skills every founder needs, and bring a teammate along.
Building for the future: AI, market fit, and knowing a winner when you see one
This is the track where the agenda gets most forward-looking, and it’s really three questions in sequence: What are you building, do people actually want it, and will it be big enough to matter?
7AI co-founder and CEO Lior Div starts with the “what.” Adding AI features to an existing product is a tactical decision, and building a company where AI is the foundation from day one is a structural one, touching everything from team composition to how go-to-market actually works. He’ll explore what founders need to rethink when AI isn’t a feature, but the premise.
Next, Kent Bennett from Bessemer Venture Partners tackles the question, “Do people want it?” This is a necessary gut check right after a session on ambitious AI-native building: It’s easy to mistake early traction or investor enthusiasm for real product-market fit. He’ll unpack the signals that genuinely indicate fit and the metrics that mislead founders into scaling too early.
Finally, TDK Ventures investment director Tina Tosukhowong zooms out to the category level with an explanation of the firm’s “King of the Hill” framework, which is the discipline top investors use to judge whether a company isn’t just viable, but also positioned to define its entire category on economics, scalability, and timing. It’s the lens that explains why some well-built, well-funded products never break out, while others soar to success.
Get ahead of the race to make the most of AI tools to build and register today.
The priceless lessons from a founder who’s seen it all
It’s one thing to hear these ideas in the abstract. HqO co-founder and CEO Chase Garbarino closes the agenda as a working example of all three tracks at once. After all, he’s raised $200 million from the right investors, scaled a team across more than 30 countries, and built a category-defining company, all without ever relocating from Boston.
He’ll break down the real advantages and disadvantages of building outside a major hub, and what every founder outside Silicon Valley should know before assuming they need to be somewhere else.

title_en: How to check if your Android phone is still getting security updates
title_fa: How to check if your Android phone is still getting security updates
excerpt_en: Your Android device will only receive updates for so long, and it might have already left its support period without you realizing.
excerpt_fa: Your Android device will only receive updates for so long, and it might have already left its support period without you realizing.
content_en:
How to check if your Android phone is still getting security updates
Your phone could be out of support even though it seems to be running fine otherwise.
Your phone doesn't blare an alarm the day it stops getting security patches; there's no banner warning or anything else like that. Support simply ends, and your device keeps working exactly as it did the day before. This can make you think everything's perfectly OK, and for a while, it is. But that false sense of security is exactly how people keep using phones that can become targets due to their outdated software.
Security updates matter more than all the fancy new features you get with Android version upgrades. While version updates add features, security patches close the vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit to steal data or install malware. A phone can look and feel fine while running for a long time without the patches that actually keep it safe.
The tricky part is that your device can't tell you whether more updates are coming; it can only show you the last one it received. Figuring out where you stand takes a little digging across a few different sources.
How to check your phone's most recent security update
Start on your phone: open Settings, tap About Phone, then look for Android version (or Software information for Samsung phones). This is where you can see the Android version, security patch date and Google Play system update status. The patch date tells you when your phone last received a fix, not whether it's still eligible for future ones. As a general rule of thumb, if the date is more than three to six months old, it's a good sign that your device could be approaching, or has already passed, its support cutoff.
It's also worth checking Settings > System > Software update, where you can see if there's an update waiting for you. You also shouldn't overlook Google Play system updates, either — these roll out separately from full OS updates and patch core components like media playback and connectivity, giving your phone extra protection between bigger releases. To do so, open the Play Store, tap your profile icon, choose Manage apps & device, then hit See details under Updates available to view the apps (including Google Play Services) that have a new version ready.
It's great that you can check all this on your phone, but none of it confirms your device's remaining support window. For that, you need to look to other sources.
How do you find your phone's end-of-life date?
Manufacturers rarely advertise an expiration date, which is where endoflife.date comes in handy. Under Operating Systems > Android OS, compare the version of Android on your device to see if it's still supported with security updates. Then, open the Device list and search by brand to pull up a table listing the exact date when each model will stop receiving security patches. The Samsung Galaxy S26 FE, for instance, will get both Android and security updates until September 2033, while the Google Pixel 6 Pro reached end of support in October 2026.
Each manufacturer has its own calendars. Google builds Android, but the manufacturer decides how long your phone gets updates for. Each one takes the Android release, builds its own interface on top (like One UI for Samsung or OxygenOS for OnePlus) and bundles in the security fixes along with its own features. That extra layer is also why updates don't land everywhere at once. Pixel phones get them faster since Google prioritizes its own hardware, while other brands need time to adapt each patch to their own software.
Manufacturers' commitment to updates differs too. A few examples:
-
Google: Pixel 8 and newer models get seven years of security and OS updates.
-
Samsung: Starting with the Galaxy S24 line and Z Fold/Flip6, the company offers seven years of support. Older Galaxy A-series and flagships from 2019 and later get four years, while some budget models stretch to six years.
-
OnePlus: For the OnePlus 12, the company offers four years of OS updates and five years of security patches. The latter is upped to six years for the OnePlus 13.
Note that these timelines apply from when the phone was first sold, not when you buy one. Interestingly, the European Union is working to make phones last longer. Starting June 2025, the EU's Ecodesign for Sustainable Product Regulation requires manufacturers to provide at least five years of software updates for new smartphones sold within the region.
What should you do if your phone has stopped getting updates?
An unsupported phone doesn't stop working, but it does become a growing liability, especially if you use it for sensitive purpose like banking apps and password managers. Replacing an old device isn't always something you can do immediately, so there are some changes you should make to limit exposure if your phone is in its last year of support or already expired.
First, to ensure your Android phone is secure, you should enable automatic app updates through Google Play to avoid security flaws within apps. Also, avoid sideloading apps from outside the Play Store. Turn on two-factor authentication for your Google account and other sensitive logins, and enable automatic backups so you don't lose data if something goes wrong. You should also run an audit on your installed apps and delete those you no longer use, while revoking sensitive permissions where they aren't strictly necessary. Avoid using public Wi-Fi networks unless you're running a VPN. In this way, you protect your data as best you can without OS updates.
If your phone's last security patch is more than six months old or you've realized you're past your model's cutoff, it's time to consider upgrading to one of the best Android phones. Pixel and Samsung flagship devices currently offer the longest update periods. Whatever you end up choosing, make sure to check its update promise before you buy so you don't have to think about this for a while.

To do so, open the Play Store, tap your profile icon, choose Manage apps & device, then hit See details under Updates available to view the apps (including Google Play Services) that have a new version ready.
It's great that you can check all this on your phone, but none of it confirms your device's remaining support window. For that, you need to look to other sources.
How do you find your phone's end-of-life date?
Manufacturers rarely advertise an expiration date, which is where endoflife.date comes in handy. Under Operating Systems > Android OS, compare the version of Android on your device to see if it's still supported with security updates. Then, open the Device list and search by brand to pull up a table listing the exact date when each model will stop receiving security patches. The Samsung Galaxy S26 FE, for instance, will get both Android and security updates until September 2033, while the Google Pixel 6 Pro reached end of support in October 2026.
Each manufacturer has its own calendars. Google builds Android, but the manufacturer decides how long your phone gets updates for. Each one takes the Android release, builds its own interface on top (like One UI for Samsung or OxygenOS for OnePlus) and bundles in the security fixes along with its own features. That extra layer is also why updates don't land everywhere at once. Pixel phones get them faster since Google prioritizes its own hardware, while other brands need time to adapt each patch to their own software.
Manufacturers' commitment to updates differs too. A few examples:
-
Google: Pixel 8 and newer models get seven years of security and OS updates.
-
Samsung: Starting with the Galaxy S24 line and Z Fold/Flip6, the company offers seven years of support. Older Galaxy A-series and flagships from 2019 and later get four years, while some budget models stretch to six years.
-
OnePlus: For the OnePlus 12, the company offers four years of OS updates and five years of security patches. The latter is upped to six years for the OnePlus 13.
Note that these timelines apply from when the phone was first sold, not when you buy one. Interestingly, the European Union is working to make phones last longer. Starting June 2025, the EU's Ecodesign for Sustainable Product Regulation requires manufacturers to provide at least five years of software updates for new smartphones sold within the region.
What should you do if your phone has stopped getting updates?
An unsupported phone doesn't stop working, but it does become a growing liability, especially if you use it for sensitive purpose like banking apps and password managers. Replacing an old device isn't always something you can do immediately, so there are some changes you should make to limit exposure if your phone is in its last year of support or already expired.
First, to ensure your Android phone is secure, you should enable automatic app updates through Google Play to avoid security flaws within apps. Also, avoid sideloading apps from outside the Play Store. Turn on two-factor authentication for your Google account and other sensitive logins, and enable automatic backups so you don't lose data if something goes wrong. You should also run an audit on your installed apps and delete those you no longer use, while revoking sensitive permissions where they aren't strictly necessary. Avoid using public Wi-Fi networks unless you're running a VPN. In this way, you protect your data as best you can without OS updates.
If your phone's last security patch is more than six months old or you've realized you're past your model's cutoff, it's time to consider upgrading to one of the best Android phones. Pixel and Samsung flagship devices currently offer the longest update periods. Whatever you end up choosing, make sure to check its update promise before you buy so you don't have to think about this for a while.

On Tuesday, Anthropic announced an expansion of its Claude for Startups program, offering subsidized access to its AI models and a variety of other benefits to qualifying companies.
The new version of the program, which launched as part of Anthropic’s SF Tech Week event, provides a free year of Claude Team, Anthropic’s paid plan for groups, with up to five premium seats, as well as $1,000 in API credits for building with Claude. Companies will also get access to Claude Marketplace, which lets them build plug-ins for the service. Companies can also book virtual office hours with Anthropic’s Applied AI team.
“We created this program because we believe the benefits of AI will reach most people through the companies that build on top of models, rather than through the models alone,” Anthropic said in an announcement. “That makes partnering closely with founders and developers central to our mission.”
Companies are eligible if they were founded in the last five years or received funding in the last two years. Interested companies can apply through the Claude for Startups program page.
