title_en: How to supercharge your Windows 11 PC with this built-in automation tool
title_fa: How to supercharge your Windows 11 PC with this built-in automation tool
excerpt_en: Task Scheduler isn't a particularly pretty part of Windows, but it's a powerful tool if you take the time to understand it.
excerpt_fa: Task Scheduler isn't a particularly pretty part of Windows, but it's a powerful tool if you take the time to understand it.
content_en:
How to supercharge your Windows 11 PC with this built-in automation tool
Windows 11 can automate more of your PC routine than its aging Task Scheduler interface suggests.
Task Scheduler has been part of Windows for years, but it's so old-school that you might have written it off. Ignore the gray menus, though, and there's a surprisingly capable automation tool underneath. Microsoft explains that Task Scheduler waits for a trigger you configure, then runs the associated task when it fires. This trigger may be a specific time, Windows startup, your login or even a system event.
Task Scheduler won't magically make your processor faster, and that's not its intended purpose. What it can do is take repetitive tasks off your hands, delay apps that normally flood Windows the moment you log in and execute commands or scripts while you're busy with something more fun. Those are pretty neat tricks for a tool that appears to have been absent from the last decade of Windows redesign meetings.
Setting up Task Scheduler is easier than it looks
To get started, type "Task Scheduler" into the Start menu and click it. You'll be greeted with a fairly busy interface; ignore most of it for now. Select Create Task in the right Actions pane. Avoid Create Basic Task; it's friendlier, but the full option reveals the controls that make Task Scheduler worth using.
From there, here's how to set up a task:
- Under General, give the task a Name.
- Open Triggers, select New and choose when to run it. Options include On a schedule, At startup or At log on.
- In Actions, choose New, then Start a program. You can direct Windows to a program, command-line tool or PowerShell.
- Review Conditions and Settings to determine whether the task can run on battery power, must wait until the PC is idle or should catch up after a missed run.
- Save it, then right-click the task in Task Scheduler Library and select Run to test it once and make sure it works.
Those conditions are of special concern to those on a laptop. According to Microsoft, a task that runs every five minutes will prevent a PC from entering a low-power idle state. Instead, you should use event, idle or maintenance triggers for tasks that do not require constant polling.
Don't enable Run with highest privileges unless the task truly needs to run as an administrator. Automation is great, but the less running as an administrator, especially without your explicit input, the better.
Three automations that are actually worth setting up
An example of putting the task manager to good use is keeping supported apps up to date with WinGet. Microsoft's package manager can check for newer versions of installed software, and winget upgrade --all
will attempt to upgrade eligible installed packages it recognizes.
You can make it a weekly task with this:
winget upgrade --all --silent --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements --disable-interactivity
Execute the command manually prior to scheduling it. Not all apps are managed by WinGet, and pinned packages are skipped by default. Some installers may still require elevation.
Another option addresses the well-known startup frenzy. Trimming unnecessary startup apps can make the logon process faster, but Task Scheduler gives you a middle ground: disable an app's normal startup entry, then launch it with a delayed logon trigger instead. A cloud storage client or other commonly used app can appear a few minutes later, rather than competing with everything else to get your desktop ready to go.
Task Scheduler also works well with PowerShell if you have scripts you've already tested, like copying files to another location or doing your own PC housekeeping. Conditions can ensure the job waits for idle time or AC power instead of barging in halfway through something important.
Power Automate for desktop is better suited to automations that require clicking through apps or interacting with interfaces. However, broader cloud and unattended automation can require paid licenses.
Also, there's little reason to automate maintenance Windows already performs itself. Storage Sense can automatically delete temporary files and items in the Recycle Bin, while Windows automatically optimizes both HDDs and SSDs.

title_en: Affordable alternatives to Nintendo's Switch 2 Pro Controller
title_fa: Affordable alternatives to Nintendo's Switch 2 Pro Controller
excerpt_en: Nintendo's best controller is expensive, so here are some cheaper, awesome alts.
excerpt_fa: Nintendo's best controller is expensive, so here are some cheaper, awesome alts.
content_en:
Affordable alternatives to Nintendo's Switch 2 Pro Controller
Nintendo's best controller is expensive, so here are some cheaper, awesome alts.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
The Switch 2 Pro Controller is an excellent gamepad, but it's pretty expensive. To be fair, we thought it was pricey when it hit the market last summer at $85, and the vibes didn't improve when it jumped to $90 just a few months later. At the time, most gaming hardware was rapidly rising in price due to a bout of illegal US tariffs, and even though Nintendo's new controller only increased by $5, it stung to suddenly be charged more money for the same product. The Switch 2 Pro Controller still costs $90 today.
That said, we get it. From the NES to the Wii U to the Switch 2, Nintendo has spent decades perfecting the gamepad, and its latest Pro Controller is its greatest result. With all of the console compatibility features you could want, sleek ergonomics and a calming matte texture, Nintendo's official Switch 2 Pro Controller is absolutely worth its asking price. It's a responsive wireless gamepad with bouncy face buttons, soft-hit thumbsticks, precise haptics, motion controls, mappable rear inputs, an audio jack and other key features, making it the obvious standard by which all other Switch 2 controllers must be judged.
Thankfully, the market is flush with less expensive but still feature-packed Switch 2 wireless gamepads from Turtle Beach, GuliKit and 8BitDo. These controllers play nicely with the Switch 2 console and offer special features like RGB lighting, cute Nintendo designs and Tunneling Magnetoresistance (TMR) analog sticks — things even the Pro Controller doesn't have. Ranging in price from $30 to $70, there's a wireless Switch 2 gamepad out there to fit your play style, aesthetic and budget.
Nintendo's Switch 2 Pro Controller
First, let's discuss the standard-setter. The $90 Switch 2 Pro Controller is supremely comfortable, it can wake up the console and it holds up just fine even after 100-plus hours of use. (Yes, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave just came out, why do you ask?). Nintendo is particularly skilled at crafting controllers that fit well in small hands, and the Switch 2 Pro is a peak example of this design ethos. It's a compact and lightweight gamepad, even with built-in HD Rumble 2, motion controls and Amiibo support, and it doesn't feel overwhelmed by the impressive amount of buttons and inputs it holds.
The official Switch 2 Pro Controller has offset analog sticks that glide like butter and barely make any noise when hitting the sides of their enclosures, thanks to a proprietary sound-dampening feature. Nintendo overhauled its thumbstick technology following an expensive drift issue with original Switch accessories, and its improved soft-hit action feels fantastic. Though they don't use Hall effect or TMR technology, the latest in anti-drift hotness, there haven't been widespread reports of drift with the Switch 2 Pro Controller or Joy-Cons. The Switch 2 Pro sticks are reactive, stealthy and well-cushioned, and they seem to stand the test of time.
The face buttons and D-pad are bouncy and responsive. Letters are printed on the face buttons rather than etched in, meaning you won't end up with a little A carved into your thumb while playing Mario Kart World, and they're slightly convex like M&Ms. The triggers and bumpers are positioned tightly together for quick transitions, and the rear buttons are mappable.
An NFC touchpoint for Amiibo connections lives underneath the Switch 2 logo on the front of the controller, above small minus, plus, home and capture buttons, and a dedicated GameChat input by the right thumbstick. The gamepad charges via a USB-C port at the top of the chassis, and there's a 3.5mm audio jack on the bottom for wired headphones. Combine that with the uber-quiet sticks, and this is easily the stealthiest controller of the bunch.
The haptics in the Switch 2 Pro are outstanding. In Resident Evil Requiem, for instance, it offers subtle feedback along the palms with your footsteps, or a barrage of pin-point vibration when bullets start flying. The soft matte texture across the controller turns the whole thing into a giant clickable worry stone, and it just feels lush.
- Haptics: Yes
- NFC support: Yes
- TMR or Hall effect sticks: No
- Motion controls: Yes
- Rear buttons: Yes
- Wake ability: Yes
- Audio jack: Yes
Best Switch 2 Pro Controller affordable alternative: 8BitDo Ultimate 2
If any company knows how to make a fantastic and reasonably priced Switch 2 controller, it's 8BitDo, the leader of the third-party gamepad market. The Ultimate 2 by 8BitDo is the controller I personally reach for when sitting down to play Switch 2: cute, remappable, super compact, satisfying to use and pretty to look at. Plus, you can set the gamepad to wake up your console with a quick shake, which is just plain fun.
The Ultimate 2 comes with a charging dock, a spare set of neon-dotted key caps and a 2.4G USB-C dongle that establishes a dedicated wireless connection between the console and controller. This dongle works with the original Switch, Switch 2 and Windows hardware, or the gamepad can connect to these devices via Bluetooth.
The haptics in the Ultimate 2 are smooth and mostly silent with customizable intensity, and you can set the rings of light around the joysticks to your liking. Mirrored metal supports reflect the RGBs at the base of the sticks, creating a second, captivating halo of light. The controller has two extra bumpers (making a total of six), two rear buttons, adjustable Hall effect triggers and TMR thumbsticks, and it's nicely tactile all around.
Not on sale, it costs $70, but you can often find it for even cheaper.
- Haptics: Yes
- NFC support: No
- TMR or Hall effect sticks: Yes
- Motion controls: Yes
- Rear buttons: Yes
- Wake ability: Yes
- Audio jack: No
Best Switch 2 Pro Controller affordable alternative for RGB freaks: Turtle Beach Afterglow

title_en: LibreOffice says ‘no AI’ is now a software feature
title_fa: LibreOffice says ‘no AI’ is now a software feature
excerpt_en: The maker of the open source document editor says it has no plans to add AI to its software's default configuration, citing user privacy.
excerpt_fa: The maker of the open source document editor says it has no plans to add AI to its software's default configuration, citing user privacy.
content_en:
If you’re looking for a document editor that doesn’t use artificial intelligence, LibreOffice may be just the software for you.
The Document Foundation, the nonprofit software maker behind the open source document editor LibreOffice, said in a blog post this week that while it does not reject AI out of hand, it “will not add” AI to its software for the foreseeable future.
The blog post comes weeks after the release of the latest version of LibreOffice in late August, in which the nonprofit reiterated that the software “contains no generative AI features.”
LibreOffice said at the time that this was a “deliberate design position” to ensure that users’ documents are not uploaded to a server for processing and that no part of the software requires a network connection to function. The nonprofit added that its software is used by tens of millions of people and organizations, and that users should retain control over their data.
“Any organisation handling confidential, legally privileged or personal data needs to know where that data goes, and the only assurance that survives an audit is that it does not leave the machine,” the organization said.
LibreOffice says users can still choose to use AI tools by installing software extensions that connect the document editor to local AI models.
The decision to eschew including AI features bucks the trend of many software makers today that try to pack in as much AI as possible, even to the detriment of the user experience. The so-called “enshittification” of modern software by packing in unnecessary and bloated features, like chatbots and AI assistants, prompted some developers to create or include features that block or remove AI features altogether.
AI tools often require the users’ data to be uploaded and processed on a remote server, which the user has no control over how the data is stored or for how long.
LibreOffice said that there is currently “no integration” that meets all of its requirements, such as ensuring that the users’ data stays on their device and that there is no reliance on a single AI provider, among other considerations. The organization’s criteria for including AI into its software is not a “definitive rejection,” but the decision was an assessment of the technology today, rather than a “judgement on the value of the sector.”
“Until then, there will be no AI of any kind in the default installation; extensions will be available for those who wish to integrate AI features, and we will closely monitor where the technology is actually heading,” said LibreOffice’s blog post.
LibreOffice is one of the many kinds of open source and alternative software used to escape the clutches of Silicon Valley tech giants.

title_en: Vinod Khosla believes ex-DeepMind engineer’s Wajo will win agent market on trust
title_fa: Vinod Khosla believes ex-DeepMind engineer’s Wajo will win agent market on trust
excerpt_en: Wajo's Fo agent can hire humans to complete a task.
excerpt_fa: Wajo's Fo agent can hire humans to complete a task.
content_en:
The personal-agent space has become closely competitive in recent weeks, with Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dot, and Instinct taking the lead and more competitors being launched each week. But Vinod Khosla is betting on former Google and DeepMind engineer Shivani Poddar’s Wajo for one simple reason: trust.
“I think the most important thing in an agent, because it’s acting for you, is trust. You have to have trust in the agent, and I think compared to either Muse or Instinct, Wajo is the most trustworthy because it is architected to focus on trust and safety first, and some of the others are not,” Khosla told TechCrunch over a call.
“I mean, who wants to give all their data to Facebook [Meta]? I don’t. And if I give my data to Facebook, I’m the product, not the product I am buying, because they are in the ad business. So trust is important, and most people don’t trust a large company like Facebook,” he added.
In broad strokes, Wajo’s Fo agent works very much like Muse or Instinct. The agent can work across iMessage and WhatsApp, and has a web interface with cards of potential tasks. Errands are organized into categories like “scheduling,” “gifting,” and “life admin.” Its agent can also call businesses or other people on your behalf, booking or canceling services as needed.
In a few early tests, I asked it to call an airline to check for upgrades, and it successfully did so. However, when I asked it to call my partner and remind her to feed the cats, the call didn’t go smoothly, and disclosures were less clear. As rivals like Instinct and Muse are also rolling out calling ability slowly, we might see more discussions around how an AI calling on someone’s behalf should disclose itself. One of the unique things about the tool is that it can hire a human to complete a task when needed.
Apart from this, Fo can create a virtual credit card and pay on your behalf without disclosing your details. The agent also has its own email and can converse with people and businesses. When websites or services block AI agents, Fo can inform the user to take action or create a group with the user and the business for verification.
The startup has also secured backing from Jeff Dean and Gokul Rajaram, but didn’t specify the money raised. Wajo didn’t provide any numbers around users but said that it’s being used in 107 countries and has grown 10x since its launch in late September.
Founder story
Prior to founding Wajo, Poddar worked in various engineering roles at Meta, Google, and DeepMind and was invovled in making the first Facebook assistant. She said that she wanted to build products that were useful to people.
“The whole journey of bringing Gemini to the world and building safety for it made me realize the technological depth that you need to do this. Google is so good in technology that sometimes it can be left behind in product. I thought I needed to do something that is both technology and product at the same time. It has to be something different, which is very grounded in what the user needs,” Poddar told TechCrunch over a call.
The former Google engineering lead mirrored Khosla’s thoughts around trust, and emphasized that it was one of the core principles for Wajo.
“Trust is something you have to build from the get-go because one of the technological things that has not been solved yet is teaching agents to unlearn. If they get access to your personal data on day zero, they will always have it for the future. I think trust needs to be built from day zero, not only in your architecture, but in product choices,” she said.
The company is doing work in a few areas in relation to trust and safety. It has applied for a patent for its virtual card system that hides users’ information from sites. For calls, the company said it will include a “trusted contact” list for users whose agents can call them. When you get a call, you can also tell the agent not to call you again, and Wajo records that preference.
The startup’s challenge is not to raise privacy concerns like other agents, especially as it is marketing safety as a core value. It also claims that despite tools like Muse being blocked by Amazon, its architecture follows the e-commerce service’s terms of service.
Wajo said that in the coming months it will explore how its Fo agent will work in social settings across multiple users, with the core idea of keeping privacy intact.

title_en: Why don't you see external antennas on mesh Wi-Fi systems?
title_fa: Why don't you see external antennas on mesh Wi-Fi systems?
excerpt_en: Mesh systems tend to look more like minimalist decor than traditional routers, and there's actually a good reason.
excerpt_fa: Mesh systems tend to look more like minimalist decor than traditional routers, and there's actually a good reason.
content_en:
Why don't you see external antennas on mesh Wi-Fi systems?
Mesh systems tend to look like minimalist decor.
In just about any space larger than an apartment, it's hard to deny the value of mesh Wi-Fi routers. They do have drawbacks — primarily their price-to-performance ratio — yet top speed is meaningless if coverage isn't consistent. You might liken it to owning a Porsche 911 in a place like the West Texas desert, where gas stations are so far apart that you could conceivably run dry on a high-speed drive.
Something we hadn't really thought about much until recently is the fact that most mesh routers are missing external antennas. They do have antennas, naturally — they're just under the surface. You'd think, though, that with coverage being a priority, gear makers would want every possible boost to signal strength.
As it turns out, burying antennas is not only fine, but actually a technical advantage given the goals of mesh systems. There are also additional business factors, although this is one case in which companies aren't cutting corners. You're likely getting a better product.
The benefits of your mesh router's internal antennas
Although external antennas do maximize range, that's actually less of a priority with mesh systems, for a reason that's glaringly obvious when you think about it for a second: A mesh network is already designed to repeat signals and fill in gaps. The most distant devices a mesh router has to talk to are usually its siblings, establishing a backhaul connection to your main router. All other devices are going to be a room or two away, at most.
Where things get interesting is the nature of internal antennas. These are often omnidirectional rather than focused, which aids in another important element of mesh technology: seamless connection and handover. With a wide net, routers can quickly detect nearby devices and switch connection duties, maintaining relatively consistent bandwidth the entire time.
In fact, there's higher potential for things to go wrong with external antennas. If they're adjustable, misaligning them can reduce connection strength to some devices. And let's not forget that external antennas are long and can be broken, whether that's during a move or by accidentally knocking a router off a tall surface. If you don't need to introduce these risks, it's logical not to.
Speaking of fragility, it's worth noting that better mesh routers may actually need more antennas than usual, since they provide a dedicated backhaul instead of splitting that bandwidth with your devices, slowing them down. A forest of external antennas would become not just more vulnerable, but unsightly and complex to manufacture. More on these points in a moment.
There are downsides to internal antennas. Apart from sacrificing range, there is hypothetically more potential for interference from nearby components. As you can tell, however, this issue has been dealt with in a way that minimizes any impact.
Boiling it down to the cool factor
Manufacturing costs offer an incentive to move things inside, too. External antennas naturally require more parts and materials. For an individual router, the price increase is going to be negligible. But spread across thousands or even millions of units, the bill quickly adds up. Considering the networking advantages, moving antennas inside is a win-win scenario for mesh Wi-Fi vendors.
Even better, internal antennas permit minimalist designs that a lot of shoppers find appealing. That's particularly important when you're going to have two or three units scattered through your home. For optimal performance, any router also needs to sit out in plain sight, and it might be easier to sell your partner on that with something that looks decorative, rather than like the radio tower it actually is.

title_en: Apple iPhone Duo vs. Motorola Razr Ultra: How do these foldables compare?
title_fa: Apple iPhone Duo vs. Motorola Razr Ultra: How do these foldables compare?
excerpt_en: The market seems to be overflowing with foldable phones, and the iPhone Duo and Moto Razr Ultra are top competitors.
excerpt_fa: The market seems to be overflowing with foldable phones, and the iPhone Duo and Moto Razr Ultra are top competitors.
content_en:
Apple iPhone Duo vs. Motorola Razr Ultra: How do these foldables compare?
Not all foldables are created equal.
It's no secret that Apple is late to the foldable phone party, but that's really its style, contrary to some myths. While it helped pioneer categories with the iPod, iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, more often than not Apple tends to sit on the sidelines, waiting for rivals like Samsung to take the big risks with new technologies. Then it swoops in, hopefully with a more polished product. The iPhone Duo is a prime example.
The foldable market is old enough at this point that Motorola has produced several generations of updated Razrs, its flagship being the 2026 Razr Ultra. At $500 less than the $2,000 iPhone Duo, there's obvious appeal, all the more so because you're not locked into the Apple ecosystem. Some of us are certainly OK with that predicament. In the Android world, though, you're not counting on one brand to get its hardware right every year.
If you're neutral on your platform pick for a future foldable, you should at least briefly pit the Ultra and Duo against each other. Given some dramatic differences, however, you're liable to end up firmly on one side of the fence. The two products are targeting very different demographics.
A battle of... passports and candybars?
The deepest split is in form factors. While both devices offer internal and external screens, with adaptable interfaces based on how they're folded, the Ultra assumes a standard candybar layout when open, measuring 7 inches diagonally. The goal is to provide a maximally compact device that's easier to slip into your pocket or a handbag, even if it means sacrificing some functions on its external screen. The Duo, meanwhile, is shaped like a passport. It operates like a regular iPhone when closed, and it opens up to provide a matte, iPad-like 7.6-inch display. It can't literally run iPad apps, but this nevertheless expands the functionality of compatible iPhone software, in some cases enabling split-screen multitasking. If you're expecting to get more work done with a foldable, the Duo wins by default.
Performance
Performance-wise, the devices are closer than you might think. We haven't benchmarked the Duo yet, since it's not shipping until October 23, but the Ultra comes equipped with a fast Snapdragon 8 Elite processor and 16GB of RAM. The Duo will likely rank faster thanks to Apple's newer A20 Pro chip and usual iOS optimizations. For the vast majority of apps, however, there shouldn't be a huge difference.
Cameras
The devices are superficially comparable in terms of cameras, with each having two rear shooters — one wide, one ultra-wide — Apple's being rated at 48 megapixels, and Motorola's at 50. The devil is in the engineering, though. iPhone cameras are typically some of the highest-rated in the industry, so we won't be surprised if the Duo continues that trend and trounces the Ultra, which has known issues versus competitors like Google's Pixel series.
On the other hand, the Ultra's front camera also slots in at 50 megapixels, whereas the Duo's is capped at 12. The Duo does have an additional under-screen internal camera, yet that may actually be worse. Apple isn't even sharing its megapixel count and is selling it primarily as a tool for FaceTime video calls. Selfie addicts are going to want to unfold and flip the Duo to use those rear sensors.
Battery and durability
The Ultra's battery lasted 31 hours in our video-based testing, and Apple claims a comparable amount for the Duo when using the internal display. Both phones should last a full day in mixed usage, in other words. Regarding toughness, both use hardened ceramic glass to protect the exposed front display; however, the Duo has a superior IP68 rating for dust and water resistance, versus the Ultra's IP48. To translate, they can both be submerged in fresh water for a short time — it's just that the Ultra is potentially vulnerable to dust particles under a millimeter. You'll probably be fine if you don't take your phone into the Sahara.
Pick your platform poison
Spec-wise, the two devices are close enough that your decision will probably boil down to three factors: price, software and use case. The Ultra's $1,500 is already too much for a lot of smartphone shoppers, never mind $2,000. You can actually spend up to $3,200 if you want to max out the Duo's storage. In theory, the Duo can replace both an iPhone and an iPad mini, so its sticker shock might have a little less sting.
If you inherently prefer iOS or Android, there's no compelling reason to switch here. The iPhone 18 Pro is available if you want a cheaper (non-folding) candybar phone, and Android fans are spoiled for book-style foldables, such as Motorola's own Razr Fold. It's probably wiser to look at that one first, particularly since $1,900 is still cheaper than $2,000. Let's not forget the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, either. The latter shares the same passport design as the Duo.
It may be worth taking a step back and questioning your reasons for getting a foldable. If you've got so little bag or pocket space that the Ultra is appealing, it might be wiser (and cheaper) to rethink your clothing and accessories. If you genuinely care about productivity, you can probably get more done by pairing an iPhone 18 Pro with a MacBook Neo, and actually save a little cash versus a Duo.

title_en: Bluesky wants to give you your own domain on the open web
title_fa: Bluesky wants to give you your own domain on the open web
excerpt_en: Bluesky says the process will still take 18-24 months, so don't expect your new, shortened 'bsky' handle any time soon.
excerpt_fa: Bluesky says the process will still take 18-24 months, so don't expect your new, shortened 'bsky' handle any time soon.
content_en:
Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider teased long-term plans on Monday when he shared that the company has applied to make “.bsky” an internet domain suffix, like .com or .org. If approved, users will be able to turn their longer social handles into shorter, cleaner domain names.
For instance, instead of @sarahp.bsky.social, my handle could one day become just “sarahp.bsky.”
That could leave Bluesky room to innovate around user profiles, turning them from a simple page that houses someone’s bio and their posts into a more comprehensive personal home page that establishes someone’s online presence.
Bluesky’s application hasn’t been approved yet. Schneider said that ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers), the nonprofit that oversees domain names for the internet, will publish the applications for the new domains on October 7, 2026, and Bluesky’s request will be among them. It’ll take 18 to 24 months for the process to be completed.
Reached for comment, Bluesky said it hasn’t finalized how .bsky domains would be requested, registered, or distributed, but the company did say it had no plans to either sell or monetize the domains.
That’s a notable decision given that domain registration can be a profitable business that could serve as a potential revenue stream for a startup that has raised significant funds but isn’t (yet?) generating ad revenue.
However, Bluesky says selling domains goes against its belief in an open web.
“Domains are a big part of the open web, as they allow users to control their own online identity,” said Rose Wang, Bluesky’s COO, in a comment shared with TechCrunch. “Bluesky was built on the belief that you should own your presence online, not rent it from a platform that can take it away.”

title_en: Emmys will move from broadcast TV to Prime Video in 2027
title_fa: Emmys will move from broadcast TV to Prime Video in 2027
excerpt_en: Non-Amazon Prime subscribers will be able to watch the awards show on the platform.
excerpt_fa: Non-Amazon Prime subscribers will be able to watch the awards show on the platform.
content_en:
Amazon announced on Tuesday that Prime Video will be the new home for the Emmy Awards, marking another major Hollywood awards show’s move from broadcast television to streaming. This will also be the first time that the ceremony has had a dedicated home, as the show rotated across broadcasters like ABC, CBS, Fox, and NBC over the past seven decades.
Prime Video will stream the awards show worldwide for six years for free, starting in 2027, where it will go live in over 240 countries and territories. Non-Amazon Prime subscribers will also be able to watch the awards show on the Prime Video platform.
The terms of the deal were not disclosed.
The move comes as the Emmys face potential viewership declines, as more of its audience moves to streaming services. This year’s ratings for the 78th primetime Emmy Awards on NBC were down nearly 10% from the year prior, after a couple of years of growth, the AP reported. However, the telecast’s 6.87 million viewers this year were higher than its all-time low of 4.3 million in January 2024.
The Emmys aren’t the only major awards show making the shift to streaming. Last year, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced a deal giving YouTube the rights to stream the Oscars beginning in 2029, while Netflix has streamed the Screen Actors Guild Awards since 2024.

title_en: Mistral’s new 1T model aims to leapfrog closed and open rivals
title_fa: Mistral’s new 1T model aims to leapfrog closed and open rivals
excerpt_en: French AI lab Mistral AI has released Mistral Large 4, a new large multimodal model aiming to leapfrog both American and Chinese rivals.
excerpt_fa: French AI lab Mistral AI has released Mistral Large 4, a new large multimodal model aiming to leapfrog both American and Chinese rivals.
content_en:
The race between open and closed AI is on, and Europe is still in the mix. On Tuesday, French AI lab Mistral AI released Mistral Large 4 (ML4), a new large multimodal model aiming to leapfrog both American and Chinese rivals — following what French president Macron described as “a third way in AI.”
Amid a growing divide between closed models that can be unplugged and open models that are often made in China, Mistral is positioning ML4 as an alternative to both. Nicknamed Le Chonk in reference to its 1 trillion parameters, ML4 is definitely not small; but is not an open-weight model yet. For the time being, it can only be accessed via a public guardrail endpoint, but Mistral plans to make its weights available in just three weeks, after safety testing is complete.
“In the meantime, we’ll work with trusted partners and governments to make sure that the open source weights can be used to defend, but not to [perform] malicious attacks,” Mistral VP Science Pierre Stock told TechCrunch.
Security concerns have been mounting in recent months, particularly among Mistral’s core audience — enterprises and institutions. At the same time, an open-weight model is easier to audit, Stock said.
Another important behind-the-scenes aspect is that ML4 was trained entirely on Mistral’s compute; using only 4,000 Nvidia GPUs “which is two to three times less than our Chinese competitors, and significantly less than the closed source competitors,” Stock said.
With benchmark results still pending, Mistral hopes ML4 will be best in class among open-weight models, especially outside of China, but not only, Stock said. Thanks to focused training, it could also outperform closed models in specific areas that are key to its customers, and where multimodal capabilities can add value.
According to Stock, ML4’s optimized use cases include cybersecurity and finance, but also chip design, which is core to two of Mistral’s main backers — Dutch giant ASML, which led its Series C, and Samsung, which led its Series D last month at a €21 billion valuation (about $24.39 billion).
At the time, the company tried to convey that its decision to host Chinese models wasn’t a pivot into becoming a mere inference provider. With Le Chonk in its corner, the company believes it should still be considered a frontier lab as well.

title_en: Controversial $110 billion mega-merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. finally closes
title_fa: Controversial $110 billion mega-merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. finally closes
excerpt_en: New media empire will be known as Skydance, with CEO David Ellision calling it a 'historic day.'
excerpt_fa: New media empire will be known as Skydance, with CEO David Ellision calling it a 'historic day.'
content_en:
Controversial $110 billion mega-merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. finally closes
New media empire will be known as Skydance, with CEO David Ellision calling it a ‘historic day.'
After nearly a year of negotiations, opposition and regulatory hurdles, the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger has finally reached its conclusion, with the $110-billion deal finally closing today.
The company now known as Skydance assumes full control of two of the largest film studios in the world, as well as networks like CBS, CNN, MTV and Comedy Central. The streaming services HBO Max and Paramount Plus also now fall under the same roof. In a press release, Skydance said that between Paramount and WBD it has committed to putting out 30 theatrical films per year, as well as more than 180 TV shows and series.
The scale of this new media empire is enormous. The combined Skydance portfolio includes DC, Harry Potter and the Game of Thrones IP, as well as the Mission: Impossible franchise, Lord of the Rings, Star Trek, Looney Tunes and SpongeBob SquarePants. TNT, Adult Swim, Cartoon Network and Nickelodeon all also now belong to the same company following completion of the merger.
Skydance will start trading on the New York Stock Exchange as SKYD today, as shares in WBD cease trading on NASDAQ. The company's total annual revenue is now nearly $70 billion, though as Variety reports, the mega-merger will immediately be saddled with $80 billion in debt.
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Skydance CEO David Ellison in a statement. "From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality."
Last week Ellison announced that his new company would adopt the name Skydance, the same name he used for the first production company he formed in 2006. The Warner Bros. acquisition comes after Skydance closed its $8 billion deal to buy Paramount last summer, and successfully fought off competition from Netflix.

title_en: The Emmy Awards are moving to Prime Video in 2027
title_fa: The Emmy Awards are moving to Prime Video in 2027
excerpt_en: Amazon is reportedly paying up to $25 million a year for exclusive global rights to the ceremony.
excerpt_fa: Amazon is reportedly paying up to $25 million a year for exclusive global rights to the ceremony.
content_en:
The Emmy Awards are moving to Prime Video in 2027
Amazon is reportedly paying up to $25 million a year for exclusive global rights to the ceremony.
Amazon has secured the exclusive rights to stream the Emmy Awards starting in 2027. You won't need to be an Amazon Prime subscriber to watch, as Prime Video will stream the ceremony for free across more than 240 counties and territories. The six-year deal with the Television Academy brings to an end the traditional annual rotation between broadcast networks ABC, CBS, FOX and NBC.
Prime Video may offer other programming from the Television Academy, such as the Hall of Fame ceremony. The Hollywood Reporter notes that it's not yet clear where viewers will be able to watch the Creative Arts Emmys going forward. Deadline reports Amazon is paying between $20 million and $25 million per year for the right to stream the main ceremony.
While there's a degree of irony in the most prestigious TV award ceremony no longer being broadcast on networks, streaming companies have been muscling into the Emmys for years. For instance, this year's best drama and comedy series winners (The Pitt and Widow's Bay) are both streaming exclusives.
The Emmys will be the first of the major entertainment award ceremonies to be broadcast exclusively on a streaming service. It's beating the Academy Awards to the punch. It was announced late last year that YouTube will be the exclusive home of the Oscars starting in 2029.

title_en: Pinterest’s AI now turns beauty Pins into action plans
title_fa: Pinterest’s AI now turns beauty Pins into action plans
excerpt_en: Pinterest’s new AI-powered Beauty Guides translate hair and nail Pins into salon terminology, with estimated costs, appointment times, and maintenance needs.
excerpt_fa: Pinterest’s new AI-powered Beauty Guides translate hair and nail Pins into salon terminology, with estimated costs, appointment times, and maintenance needs.
content_en:
Pinterest on Tuesday showed off a new feature that will leverage AI to take action on your saved inspiration from beauty-related Pins, like hair and nail ideas, and turn them into actionable plans you can take with you to the salon.
“Beauty Guides,” which are powered by the company’s visual intelligence and generative AI technology, Pinterest Intelligence, will translate Pins into terms and phrases used by stylists and nail artists that everyday users may not know, like “balayage,” “root melt,” or “almond nails.”
The feature is a small but practical way to introduce AI into users’ everyday lives, as it slots into something that people are already doing: bringing a photo of their inspiration to the salon. That’s useful to a large extent, but having the right terminology at hand while you discuss what parts of the look you want to edit or change can be useful as well.
Plus, the guides offer the sort of information that can help users plan for their visit, like the time each part of the process may take and the cost. (Balayage goes into the hundreds of dollars, so that’s information you might like to have up front!)
The action guides will show up when you tap on the “Get the Guide” button within the app, and will then offer details about what, specifically, you should ask for to achieve the same look, the time it takes, price range, and maintenance requirements, like how often you’ll need to trim, tone, or touch up, for instance.
At launch, the feature will work across Pins related to hairstyle, color, nail shape, and finish.

content_en:
Confession: When BougeRV told me about its remote-controlled wagon with animated lighting, I called it in for a laugh, expecting to eviscerate it in a review. It’s ridiculous, to be sure. But the DuneRover also proved very capable, with enough torque to flatten hills even when carrying over 200 pounds of gear. It can also traverse soft sand that defeats conventional wagons.
This remote-controlled wagon is silly but so very useful
BougeRV’s DuneRover is so good on hills and sand that you’ll forgive the disco lights.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
As someone who regularly uses a variety of wagons to haul all sorts of gear, the DuneRover is an epiphany. But what BougeRV sent me was a Kickstarter prototype — and it shows.
Production units won’t ship until February 2027. So, what follows is less of a review and more a risk assessment for those considering backing the Kickstarter. That way, you can decide whether it makes sense to lock down early-bird pricing at $467, a claimed 48 percent discount off the eventual $899 list price. (Though I’ll wager it’ll always be sold for some kind of discount.)
Frankly, $500 isn’t outlandish for a wagon. Prices start at around $40 for a rickety model that will only last a few months, $300 for something durable from a reputable brand, and closer to $800 at the top end. And none of those wagons provides a motorized assist.
Let’s begin with the dumb stuff. The wagon has LED light bars on the back that are on by default and could come in handy at a campsite after dark. You can turn them off via the app, but you have to do it every time you restart the wagon. The default for a battery-powered device used primarily during the day should obviously be off.
Then there’s the remote control. I think I know what happened here. The product designers had a choice: route a cable through all the folding mechanisms that separate the motor from the handle or make it wireless. Wireless won, and then someone from marketing said, ‘Hey, I’ve got an idea!’
I mean, a remote-controlled wagon is so absurd that it’s kind of fun, and it brought a lot of joyful finger-pointing to onlookers during my testing. Maybe that’s enough?
The DuneRover is no joke for hauling gear. It’s fitted with two brushless geared motors, each producing up to 400W of output and up to 33Nm of torque. The wagon is activated by a trigger embedded in the handle that you press naturally when you pull the cart. Walk faster and the wagon will roll faster. Sometimes the wagon will lurch forward on that initial pull before settling into your walking rhythm. It’s not dangerous, it’s just unexpected. Release the trigger on the handle, and the wagon stops, even on an incline.
Pulling an oversized load weighing over 200 pounds up a 10 percent grade required a modicum of effort — but just a tenth of what it would have taken without the motor assist. Even on that steep incline, the wagon stops (with an inch or two of rollback) just as soon as I let go of the trigger. Repeated stopping and starting on slopes did, however, seem to confuse the DuneRover, occasionally causing the motors to become jerky as soon as I started walking again. A simple on/off resumed normal operation.
The motors also regulate speed when walking downhill with a heavy load. With the trigger held down, the controller did a good job monitoring changes in acceleration and countering the wagon’s speed to maintain my walking pace. When I stopped, so did the wagon, even on that 10 percent grade with a 200-plus pound load.
The motors aren’t powerful enough to haul that same load through soft sand, however. The oversized beach wheels performed much better in sand with loads weighing about half that, and should be excellent for families carrying a cooler, snacks, beach umbrella, toddler, and toys for a day at the beach.
I like that the DuneRover easily transformed depending on what I needed to haul. The sides can be unzipped and folded flat to convert the wagon into a cart for hauling oversized items or a senior dog. You can also unzip the sides but leave the straps connected to create more volume inside the wagon. I used this configuration a lot. Just know that you’ll want to bring a few bungee cords or cargo nets to keep everything securely in place.
My prototype suffered from intermittent rolling resistance with the motor off. The wagon would roll along fine for five or six feet, but then the wheels attached to the motors would brake, drag along the ground, and then release after a second or two. BougeRV assures me this isn’t something that would be exhibited by its production wagons. I ended up just leaving the motor on throughout my testing, even when I didn’t need it. The 82.14Wh battery was more than up to the challenge.
I used the DuneRover to move gear out of a beach house along the same route where I tested BougeRV’s original electric wagon. Six times I pulled the DuneRover along a path with 5 percent grade on one end and a 10 percent grade on the other. After six kilometers (3.73 miles) of soft sand, hard asphalt, wooden ramps, and gravel, the battery still showed a 74 percent charge. Not bad.
The removable battery features a bi-directional 100W USB-C port, making it a rather capable power bank. It can also charge from a 100W solar panel plugged into its XT-60 jack, thanks to a built-in MPPT solar controller. The battery in my prototype is not protected against rain, so I tested it in dry conditions, though BougeRV promises “full-vehicle IPX6-rated protection” in the production wagon.
The DuneRover is a beast at 59.5 pounds (27kg) with the battery and wheels installed. It’s also rather chunky when it folds. The quick-release front wheels can be removed if a flatter pack is required.
Overall, I’m impressed with the prototype DuneRover I tested — it’s capable, versatile, and proved to be an enormous help over the last few weeks of moving things between a holiday home, home, and adventure...

title_en: Common mistakes you should avoid when using foldable phones
title_fa: Common mistakes you should avoid when using foldable phones
excerpt_en: Foldable phones have unique durability concerns thanks to their moving parts and internal screens.
excerpt_fa: Foldable phones have unique durability concerns thanks to their moving parts and internal screens.
content_en:
Common mistakes you should avoid when using foldable phones
Your phone can fold in half, but your keys shouldn’t join it.
The most common mistake you should avoid when using foldable phones is dropping them. But that's common knowledge and doesn't make for a very exciting discussion. You're probably thinking about the inside foldable screen, where the most common way to damage it is closing it on something that shouldn't be there. Samsung's foldable care page warns that cards, coins or keys can scratch or even puncture a Galaxy foldable's inner display.
That seems straightforward enough; just make sure your car keys aren't sitting on top of your phone when you try to close it. But if you work a particularly dirty job or live near the beach, that complicates matters. You can't always spot dirt easily, and beach sand will find its way into absolutely anything.
Keep in mind that not all foldables are on equal footing. Some foldable screens are a bit softer and weaker than others. The Galaxy Z Fold8 and Fold8 Ultra, for instance, have an IP48 rating, whereas the new iPhone Duo boasts an IP68. The first digit describes the degree of protection against solid objects; a 4 means objects 1mm thick or larger can't enter, while 6 indicates a dust-tight device.
Treat the inner screen with care
A foldable's inner screen is far from a conventional slab-phone display. It has to fold, after all, so don't assume you can press on it as firmly as you would on a standard phone's outer glass. That includes actions you've probably done without thinking, like scratching a speck from the screen with your nail.
Another mistake is peeling off a factory-applied inner screen film because it looks like disposable shipping protection. This was surprisingly easy to do early on, but now the edges are tucked in and better hidden. Samsung highly recommends leaving these protective layers alone. On the flipside, don't stick an unapproved screen protector over a foldable display. These phones aren't like their slab cousins, so any old screen protector won't do. Only use a protector or stylus the manufacturer specifically lists as compatible with that model.
You don't have to baby a foldable phone, though it may seem that way coming from a traditional smartphone. These precautions just require you to be a little more particular when handling the folding screen. Avoid any concentrated force or closing it on anything other than open air.
What is the lifespan of a foldable phone?
There is no specific lifespan for foldables, though there are suggestions and indicators. For instance, we know that manufacturers test the hinges and screens by folding the phones between 200,000 and 500,000 times. If you open your phone 100 times a day, that would be 5 to 10 years.
However, that's not a guarantee. Samsung claimed the Galaxy Z Fold7's display remained functional after 500,000 folds in lab testing. Sounds pretty reassuring, but a controlled test doesn't mean the Fold7 would survive that many opens and closes throughout your daily life. In the past, Samsung's claim of 200,000 folds on the original Galaxy Fold fell short. When you hear figures tossed around, treat them as general benchmarks and marketing numbers.
Besides, it's far more useful to check for dirt before you close the phone than to count your folds each day. Don't push heavily on the display or use the wrong stylus. Use a soft cloth to clean marks on the screen instead of digging at them with your fingernail. And while the IP68 rating sounds great, Apple notes that the iPhone Duo's water and dust resistance may diminish with normal wear. Nothing lasts forever, but wear increases faster when moving parts are involved.

You don't have to baby a foldable phone, though it may seem that way coming from a traditional smartphone. These precautions just require you to be a little more particular when handling the folding screen. Avoid any concentrated force or closing it on anything other than open air.
What is the lifespan of a foldable phone?
There is no specific lifespan for foldables, though there are suggestions and indicators. For instance, we know that manufacturers test the hinges and screens by folding the phones between 200,000 and 500,000 times. If you open your phone 100 times a day, that would be 5 to 10 years.
However, that's not a guarantee. Samsung claimed the Galaxy Z Fold7's display remained functional after 500,000 folds in lab testing. Sounds pretty reassuring, but a controlled test doesn't mean the Fold7 would survive that many opens and closes throughout your daily life. In the past, Samsung's claim of 200,000 folds on the original Galaxy Fold fell short. When you hear figures tossed around, treat them as general benchmarks and marketing numbers.
Besides, it's far more useful to check for dirt before you close the phone than to count your folds each day. Don't push heavily on the display or use the wrong stylus. Use a soft cloth to clean marks on the screen instead of digging at them with your fingernail. And while the IP68 rating sounds great, Apple notes that the iPhone Duo's water and dust resistance may diminish with normal wear. Nothing lasts forever, but wear increases faster when moving parts are involved.

title_en: Can a MacBook handle heavy games? Here's what you should know
title_fa: Can a MacBook handle heavy games? Here's what you should know
excerpt_en: macOS is now a far healthier platform for gaming than it was just a few years ago, but it can't compete with Windows in many ways.
excerpt_fa: macOS is now a far healthier platform for gaming than it was just a few years ago, but it can't compete with Windows in many ways.
content_en:
Can a MacBook handle heavy games? Here's what you should know
The gap between Mac and PC is finally closing, but be careful before you pick a Mac as your primary gaming platform.
Macs have never exactly been gaming machines. For a long time, not only was the hardware lacking, but many developers never bothered to bring their titles to macOS. But the situation is different now with Apple silicon — the M-series chips are powerful, and there are new tools to easily port PC games to Mac.
But can a MacBook really handle demanding games? Technically, it can, but there are many other factors you should consider before choosing a Mac as your gaming machine. Yes, the gaming landscape on macOS is much better now than it was six years ago, but there's still a huge gap between Macs and Windows PCs.
What a MacBook can and can't handle
Thanks to Apple silicon, hardware is no longer a Mac's weak point. If you have one of the latest Macs, such as an M5 MacBook Pro, it will likely run most games well — even some big names you might not have expected. Apple lists Assassin's Creed Shadows, Dead Island 2 and Cyberpunk 2077 as some of the titles a Mac can run natively. The list of Mac-compatible games has been growing a lot, with more and more titles coming to macOS alongside their Windows versions.
And even if your favorite game doesn't have a macOS port, there may still be an alternative. Apple has created something called the Gaming Porting Toolkit, which helps developers port Windows games to macOS using native translations. While this tool is intended for developers, anyone can use it to run PC games on a Mac with just a few lines of code. I've been using it to run GTA V on my M4 Pro MacBook Pro, and the results are pretty solid; I can get a steady 60 frames per second with high graphics settings. It's not perfect and there are a few glitches here and there, but it works well overall for a game being translated in real-time.
If you're not sure which games your Mac can run, it's worth checking out MacGamingDB. This is a community-run website that provides compatibility details for thousands of titles, making it easy to quickly find out how your favorite game performs on a specific Mac model. It saves you a lot of time, since you don't have to download gigabytes of data just to find out the game doesn't work.
Which MacBook to buy, and when to look elsewhere
If you really want to game on a MacBook, the MacBook Pro is your best option. Even the base model with the M5 Pro chip and 24GB of RAM gives you enough power to run most modern games smoothly. If you need more, you can upgrade it with an M5 Max chip, which adds more RAM and a better GPU.
Of course, don't expect a MacBook Neo to perform the same as the latest MacBook Pro line. Both the MacBook Neo and the MacBook Air have less powerful processors and no internal fan, which makes them less suitable for running demanding games. They can still run some titles, but performance won't be ideal and you'll have to lower the resolution and graphics settings a bit.
But if you're serious about gaming, you should probably buy a PC instead. A Windows PC will likely cost you less for the same graphical power, and it will run all games natively without you having to worry about compatibility issues. You might also want to check out cloud gaming services like GeForce NOW or Xbox Cloud Gaming to stream games on your MacBook, so hardware won't be an issue. You just need a good internet connection.

excerpt_en: Google may be expanding its "Call for Me" AI feature beyond business calls so you can use it to send messages to friends and family. Android Authority reports finding a "Gemini Calling" introductory screen in an APK teardown with examples that include "Call Mom and tell her I...
excerpt_fa: Google may be expanding its "Call for Me" AI feature beyond business calls so you can use it to send messages to friends and family. Android Authority reports finding a "Gemini Calling" introductory screen in an APK teardown with examples that include "Call Mom and tell her I...
content_en:
Google may be expanding its “Call for Me” AI feature beyond business calls so you can use it to send messages to friends and family. Android Authority reports finding a “Gemini Calling” introductory screen in an APK teardown with examples that include “Call Mom and tell her I will be 15 minutes late” and “Call John and ask if he is coming for dinner.”
Gemini Call for Me might tell your mom you’re running late
A rumored Android update would automate personal phone calls with Gemini AI.
A rumored Android update would automate personal phone calls with Gemini AI.
Based on those examples, even with this expansion, Gemini would likely be limited to basic, text message-like calls. While Google’s AI might not automate an entire catch-up phone call with your relatives, it could deliver quick messages to people who prefer a phone call, miss texts often, or even still have a landline phone.
Android Authority also says it found “granular permissions” for Gemini actions in individual apps, including what appear to be settings for phone call permissions. These settings would allow users to pick and choose which app capabilities they want to allow Gemini to access, potentially giving users an option to opt out of receiving incoming automated calls from Gemini. However, as Android Authority notes, it’s also possible Google might not publicly release this expansion or the granular Gemini app settings.

title_en: Mini PC vs. laptop: Which is better for your home office?
title_fa: Mini PC vs. laptop: Which is better for your home office?
excerpt_en: Mini PCs offer a convenient form factor, but a laptop is ready to go with you anywhere. There's no perfect answer.
excerpt_fa: Mini PCs offer a convenient form factor, but a laptop is ready to go with you anywhere. There's no perfect answer.
content_en:
Mini PC vs. laptop: Which is better for your home office?
A laptop can become a desktop with one cable, making the home-office choice less obvious than it looks.
I own both a mini PC and a laptop, and I prefer to have the mini PC on my desk. It doesn't take up much space and fades into a setup that revolves around the monitor, keyboard and mouse I actually use. The small box becomes a part of the office and an organized desk.
However, a laptop can do the same. Plug one into a big screen via HDMI, throw in a wireless keyboard and mouse, and the basic experience is pretty close. This can get even better with a compatible USB-C or Thunderbolt dock to manage displays, peripherals, networking and charging all in one. When both computers are set up at a desk, the gap between them becomes tiny.
What you're paying for and whether the computer needs to leave that desk are the more important questions.
Mini PCs are often closer to laptops than desktops
While their name implies a desktop PC that's been hit with a shrink ray, there are plenty of mini PCs based on hardware that would be perfectly normal in a laptop. For instance, the ASUS NUC 15 Pro supports Intel's Core Ultra 7 265H (a mobile processor), along with SO-DIMM memory and M.2 SSD storage.
There's a practical explanation for that. When you're attempting to fit a whole computer into a box that's small enough to fit behind a monitor, laptop components are quite convenient. But similar parts don't guarantee identical performance. Cooling, firmware and manufacturer-set power limits all have an impact on what a processor can sustain, especially when you put it to work for more than a quick benchmark. Thus, two machines with the same CPU name can still behave differently.
Upgradeability varies too, which is one of the main downsides of a mini PC. The NUC 15 Pro offers two SO-DIMM slots and two M.2 storage slots on supported configurations, offering greater flexibility for memory and storage upgrades than some thin laptops with soldered memory. Not all configurations include memory or storage from ASUS, however.
That last detail is important for fair price comparisons. When you start adding RAM, an SSD and perhaps an operating system to the list of items, a bargain-looking barebones mini PC can turn into less of a value.
The same reality check applies to graphics. Integrated graphics are just fine for email, office apps, video calls and browser-intensive tasks. If you're doing demanding video editing, 3D work or any other GPU-intensive task, don't assume that the small desktop box has more graphics power than a laptop.
A docked laptop makes this a much tougher choice
A mini PC has straightforward appeal compared to a laptop: you're buying the computer without the built-in screen, battery, keyboard and trackpad that may go unused for the majority of its lifespan. That's largely why I enjoy mine. I prefer to have a machine that's part of the workspace and always available. But a laptop has a pretty good response to that argument, and it's a single cable.
With a compatible docking station, a laptop can connect to external displays, Ethernet, a keyboard, mouse and other USB devices simultaneously. Supported models can also be powered from the same dock (specific capabilities vary by laptop and dock). Close the lid, tuck the machine into a stand and your day-to-day setup can feel like one built around a mini PC.
The difference is evident when you have to travel. Unplug the laptop and the same computer comes with you, including your local files, apps, browser sessions and settings. There's only one machine to maintain — no need to wonder which computer has the document you definitely saved five minutes before a meeting.
But that doesn't mean a laptop is the obvious home-office option. Mini PCs can be compact, flexible and even more cost-effective if your computer doesn't move around much and you already have a monitor and peripherals. If you're a frequent traveler, work in various locations or want to keep everything on one machine, a docked laptop might be the better choice.

title_en: How to add and customize your CarPlay widgets
title_fa: How to add and customize your CarPlay widgets
excerpt_en: CarPlay's widgets let you check info quickly, which is a great option for apps that aren't otherwise supported.
excerpt_fa: CarPlay's widgets let you check info quickly, which is a great option for apps that aren't otherwise supported.
content_en:
How to add and customize your CarPlay widgets
Personalizing your CarPlay dashboard beyond its apps only takes a few easy steps.
Since Apple added widgets to CarPlay in iOS 26, compatible cars have gotten even closer to being a proper extension of your iPhone. Instead of being limited to navigation, messaging and audio, CarPlay widgets let you view information from many other apps on your phone. Whether you want to check live game scores, manage your smart home or follow the forecast at your destination, a widget makes it simple to do so on the road.
Before diving in, you should know there's a difference between a CarPlay app and a widget. An app like Maps or Spotify is fully optimized for CarPlay and takes up most, if not all, of your display for easier interaction. On the other hand, widgets appear in customizable stacks and provide specific details from the app they represent.
Luckily, customizing your CarPlay experience, including widgets, is straightforward. And even better, iOS 27 expanded the available widget pool beyond what was possible before.
How to start adding widgets to CarPlay
While you're parked or not driving, open the Settings app on your iPhone, then go to General > CarPlay and tap your car. Next, select Widgets. Make sure Show Widgets is enabled, then select Add Widget to browse your options.
You'll see recommended choices at the top, followed by a list of compatible apps on your phone. A given app can offer multiple widgets, so make sure to explore them all. The number of widgets that show at a time changes based on the size of your car's infotainment center.
Removing or rearranging widgets is simple. From the same page, use the handles on the right side to drag items and adjust your layout, or hit the red minus button to remove anything you don't want anymore. Some widgets will show a blue i icon to customize them, such as picking one of your saved locations in the Weather app.
At the bottom of the Settings page, you can also toggle some automation options. Turning on Smart Rotate will change to the most relevant widget in a stack based on factors like the time or your location, while Widget Suggestions will display potentially useful ones even if you haven't manually added them.
To access your widgets while on the road, swipe from left to right and you'll find them on the leftmost page. Swipe up or down on a stack to move through them as needed.
Recommended widgets for CarPlay
Widgets can fill gaps that CarPlay apps aren't able to, so there are lots of ways to put them to use. If you ever feel homesick on long trips, add the Photos widget and select any album to show. Meanwhile, if you take full advantage of Apple HomeKit and are worried that you may have left a lamp on, you can turn it off using a Home widget.
Additional first-party options include Reminders, Weather, Clock and Podcasts. An analog clock looks fancy when you don't need navigation, while Weather can tell you when the sun will set or rise. Apple Sports is also an option for following your favorite teams as you drive.
Many third-party widgets offer unique additions to your dashboard, especially after iOS 27's expansion. You can see what your friends are up to using Instagram stories or add the Amazon widget to check your order status and make sure you're home in time. If you're in need of an AI voice assistant in the car, you can utilize widgets for chatbots like Claude and Gemini.
Some widgets are certainly more useful than others; you likely don't need to check your Duolingo streak or see LinkedIn updates while driving. For best results, stick to widgets that provide easily glanceable, non-distracting info.

title_en: Are extended warranties on TVs and laptops ever really worth it?
title_fa: Are extended warranties on TVs and laptops ever really worth it?
excerpt_en: TV and laptop repairs can get expensive in a hurry, so getting a warranty sounds smart. But is it really?
excerpt_fa: TV and laptop repairs can get expensive in a hurry, so getting a warranty sounds smart. But is it really?
content_en:
Are extended warranties on TVs and laptops ever really worth it?
Or are they just another useless upsell?
Have mercy on retail clerks. To keep their jobs, they're often asked to push promotions they know most customers don't want, such as memberships and credit cards. Upselling looks good on a manager's ledger, even if it irritates a good portion of their customers.
If you've been shopping for smart TVs, laptops or just about any major piece of electronics in the past decade, you've no doubt been pitched on the idea of an extended warranty, AppleCare+ and Best Buy Protection being a couple of familiar examples. At a glance, they're more reasonable than most in-store promotions. Everything breaks eventually, and the cost of some repairs can be eye-watering. Just ask anyone who's smashed the display on their MacBook.
Despite this, you can safely skip an extended warranty in most circumstances. They mostly exist for the sake of an upsell, which you can tell by the strings attached and the fundamental nature of consumer electronics. When an extended plan is justified, you'll likely know before you walk in the door.
Why extended warranties are usually a waste of money
For starters, extended warranties are typically focused around defects, and any TV, laptop or similarly expensive device is likely to be covered by the manufacturer for 90 days to a year or more. This matters because if a product is defective, it's going to fail under relatively normal strain, by definition. You're liable to find out quickly if it's faulty, though there are obviously outliers.
Another point is that while planned obsolescence is real, a product that survives the first year is likely to survive past the two- or three-year window that's common for many extended warranties. In an accelerated longevity test by RTINGS, 102 TVs were run nonstop between November 2022 and September 2025. Only two actually failed before they reached 3,000 hours, and most made it to at least 8,000. This longevity test employed TVs that had already been used for hundreds of hours, so the results didn't show an initial spike for models that failed right away — a spike that would be present if the TVs were all brand-new. But again, those failures often are covered by the manufacturer and wouldn't require an extended warranty. If you watched TV for four hours a day, every day, it would take you over two years to reach that 3,000-hour mark, by which point just 2 percent of the TVs had failed.
Unbiased reliability figures are harder to come by for laptops, but it almost doesn't matter for a couple of reasons. The first is that planned obsolescence factor. Within two or three years, just about any device you buy — especially a laptop — is going to be supplanted by something with improved performance for a similar price. Meanwhile, equivalent products are going to become cheaper and cheaper, especially if you're willing to buy a used or refurbished model.
That factors into the second point, which is the cost of an extended warranty vs. just saving up for a replacement or repair. To cover a $1,300 TV, for example, Best Buy charges approximately $160 for two years of Geek Squad TV Protection, and $280 for five years. While the cost of replacing the display panel could vastly exceed either sum, the retailer estimates that other repairs will typically fall between $255 and $395. You could spend most or all of the cost of a repair on a warranty you may never use, and you'll still be stuck with old hardware if you successfully pursue a claim.
Some warranties include loopholes, on that note. We can't make blanket statements, but it's important to watch out for clauses that prevent you from seeking repairs if there are signs of liquid exposure or anything else that could be branded user error, regardless of whether it's the source of your problems. In other situations, you may be forced to use a manufacturer's warranty first if it's still in effect, Geek Squad Protection being a prime example.
When does an extended warranty actually make sense?
Though TVs are rarely mission-critical, there are professionals who simply can't afford any downtime with a laptop or other productivity tools, and put the equipment they own through the wringer. The cost of an extended warranty is nothing by comparison, though if you're in this camp, it's essential that you pick a plan that allows for loaner units or rapid repairs or replacements. In fact, you may be looking at special business-oriented warranties that aren't pitched over the checkout counter.
If you hate the idea of downtime but you're not necessarily a professional, it can make sense to invest in a plan like AppleCare+. That incorporates theft and loss replacements for some devices and vastly reduced prices for fixing accidental damage, including liquids. Considering that many cities have an Apple Store or at least an authorized service site, same-day repairs and replacements are a real possibility.
Unfortunately, most vendors don't have such an extensive support network. If you need a repair, there's a strong chance your device is going to be shipped to a depot in another city, then back a few days later. And they may ship it back unrepaired if they can't replicate the issue you reported — something we've experienced directly. Every warranty is a gamble, in that respect.
