title_en: Siri can index more of your personal data —  here's how to limit it
title_fa: Siri can index more of your personal data —  here's how to limit it
excerpt_en: If you're concerned about Apple's new digital assistant, here's how you can restrict its access to your data.
excerpt_fa: If you're concerned about Apple's new digital assistant, here's how you can restrict its access to your data.
content_en:
Siri can index more of your personal data — here's how to limit it
If you’re concerned about Apple’s new digital assistant, here’s how you can restrict its access to your data.
With the release of iOS 27, Apple has finally begun rolling out its long delayed redesign of Siri. You'll need to join a waitlist before you can get Siri AI, but once you gain access to the new digital assistant, you're likely to find it's a significant leap over its predecessor. Engadget's Mat Smith found the new Siri much improved when he tested it on the iOS 27 beta, thanks to its ability to deliver smarter, more personalized responses.
However, there is a downside worth mentioning. Apple partnered with Google to train the new large language models that power Siri AI's features. And as with any AI system, the new Siri requires a great deal of data to work at its best, and that data comes from you(r phone).
How does Siri AI access data from your apps?
The reason Siri AI can provide a more personalized experience is thanks to a framework called App Intents that allows Apple Intelligence tools, including Siri, to access data from the apps on your Apple devices. When you enable Siri AI on your iPhone, iPad or Mac, Spotlight and Siri are unified under a single interface. By default, when you ask Siri a question, it will search through your Apple apps, including Notes and Messages, to pull information that might be relevant to your prompt or query. If a developer has chosen to support App Intents, Siri will be able to scan through their apps too.
Siri AI relies on a combination of on-device models and Apple's Private Cloud Compute (PCC) infrastructure, meaning the assistant will sometimes offload your data to a remote server for processing. Apple says it does not store any data sent to its PCC servers after processing a request, and that it can't even see the data. Still, you might feel uncomfortable about sharing data regardless. Thankfully, there are ways you can control what Siri can index.
Restrict Siri AI's access to content inside your apps
As mentioned, Apple has left it up to developers to decide if Siri AI can access the data people generate inside of their apps. That means as long as they allow iOS 27's Spotlight tool to index the contents of their apps, Siri AI can in turn access and surface that information for you as a user. However, you still have control over the process, and can ultimately decide to restrict Siri from accessing your apps. To do so, follow these steps:
- Open the Settings app.
- Scroll down and tap Apps.
- Select the app you want to restrict Siri from accessing.
- Tap Search.
- Toggle off Show Content in Search.
After you disable Show Content in Search in relation to a particular app, Siri won't pull information from that app, even if you ask it to do so directly. For example, if you disable indexing of Messages, and ask Siri to summarize a series of messages from your friend, the digital assistant will tell you it can't find those messages.
In the Apps settings menu, you may have noticed a collection of options grouped under "Apple Intelligence & Siri." For the purposes of this guide, you can leave those alone; they don't have privacy implications. Instead, they primarily control where iOS might suggest an app for you. For instance, if you disable the "Suggest App" option, you won't see that specific app among the "Siri Suggestions" iOS generates when you access your iPhone's search shade. The "Learn from this App" option sounds nefarious, but it merely allows iOS to see how and when you're using your apps so that it can tailor when it surfaces those apps for you.
On-screen awareness
Even after you restrict Siri's ability to search through your apps, you can still get it to help you with situations requiring contextual knowledge on a more ad-hoc basis. A feature called on-screen awareness allows Siri to read the contents of screenshots and images. This can be useful from an accessibility standpoint, or if you want Siri to summarize a lengthy article or message thread. Just note if you snap a screenshot and ask Siri to interpret it, it might be sent to the company's PCC servers.
Ensure you're not sharing Siri recordings with Apple
By default, Apple won't collect or use the data from your interactions with Siri to train future versions of the virtual assistant. But as part of your iPhone's setup process, you might have accidently opted into sharing your Siri recordings and transcripts with the company. Either way, it's worth checking to confirm your Siri data isn't being used for model training.
- Open the Settings app.
- Tap Privacy & Security.
- Scroll down and select Analytics & Improvements.
- Disable Improve Siri & Dictation if turned on.
Disable Siri AI altogether
One final option worth mentioning is that you can revert to the older version of Siri. This gives you a way to continue using apps like CarPlay with your voice while limiting your privacy exposure. Unintuitively, however, you'll find the option to do this hidden inside the Screen Time section.
- Open the Settings app.
- Tap Screen Time, followed by Content & Privacy Restrictions.
- Enable Content & Privacy Restrictions.
- Tap Siri.
- Under Allowed Siri Version, select Siri Classic.
Alternatively, you can disable Siri entirely by following the steps below.
- Open the Settings app.
- Tap Siri.
- Scroll down and select Turn off Siri.
If you want to restrict any other part of the Apple Intelligence suite, Apple has helpful support page on the topic.

title_en: Can Safeworld convince people that GenAI robots won’t hurt them?
title_fa: Can Safeworld convince people that GenAI robots won’t hurt them?
excerpt_en: Safeworld is building digital humans to make sure robots don't hurt the real ones.
excerpt_fa: Safeworld is building digital humans to make sure robots don't hurt the real ones.
content_en:
The big trend in robots is handing the keys over to a generative AI model, but that brings with it a problem: that architecture isn’t predictable the way traditional algorithms are. How can you be sure your brand new humanoid will be safe?
Dr. Ding Zhao, who directs the Safe AI lab at Carnegie Mellon University, has been working on this problem for almost his entire career. Now, along with veteran startup executive Kyle Wong and machine learning engineer Simo Rachidi, he’s founded a company, Safeworld, intended to solve it.
“The safety challenge that we’re talking about is a combination of, one, really advanced generative AI probabilistic evals — how do you underwrite the risk of a probabilistic system?” Zhao says. “The second part that’s really hard is the trust part, and you need both to deploy a robot.”
Safeworld is emerging from stealth today with a seed round of more than $12 million, led by Shine Capital and a16z Speedrun, with additional investment from Box Group, Carnegie Mellon University Endowment, Innovation Endeavors and SV Angel.
“The time to build an industry safety standard is now while robots are being designed and deployed,” a16z Speedrun partner Jonathan Lai told TechCurnch. “By the time you have robots in households colliding with kids and causing safety incidents, that’s way too late.”
Safeworld’s specialty is evaluating a robotic control system in simulations that are populated with realistic human models. It’s akin to the challenge faced by companies like Tesla or Wayve, which must ensure that their vehicles respond appropriately to a variety of surprising incidents they may encounter on the road. But that will be more difficult for robots, Zhao argues, because they work in unstructured environments, and because each facility they are in will have different safety standards.
“One of the most common areas is if there is a blind corner in this particular factory,” Wong said. “What is the speed or what is the stopping distance that you need to make sure that this robot will not collide with a particular human? If a human is carrying boxes, for example, will the robot detect the human or not?”
To answer that question, Safeworld will build a digital version of that corner in a model like Genesis or MuJoCo, insert a simulation of the robot it is evaluating, driven by its real software, and then run thousands of scenarios where human models encounter the robot. That’s harder than it seems, per Zhao, because people are unpredictable.
“Tripping and falling is also a good example of something that we do a lot of testing with the simulation,” Wong said. “Otherwise, you would have to go and trip and fall for the robot, which is like a hard thing to be doing all the time.”
There are definite similarities between the platform that Safeworld is building and the tools being used internally by robot builders. The founders, however, believe that beyond their specific expertise, robot-makers will want a third-party to validate their work, if only to share information about safety cases between competitors.
“A lot of people are underestimating how hard some of these edge cases are going to be to solve,” Zhao said. “It is not the robot in the vacuum, in the demo, that we are worried about. It is the robot that is deployed at scale, with people who potentially never operated a robot before.”
Vishal Dugar, the CTO of Gritt Robotics, is developing the AI brain for robots that currently help workers install photovoltaic panels at industrial-scale solar farms, and aspires to take on more complex construction tasks. His company is partnering with Safeworld as they develop their safety simulations.
“The difficulty with most of our systems is it’s very hard to formally prove it by doing some math, writing some equations, and saying yeah, the system is verified to be safe,” Dugar says. “It necessarily has to be done empirically.”
His robots operate alongside human workers, and ensuring that a robotic arm doesn’t hit them is obviously top of mind. To verify that in practice requires considering all kinds of potential scenarios.
“Humans have many kinds of appearances,” Dugar points out. “Their bodies can be in different configurations. They could be kneeling, standing. They could be tripping and falling potentially. They could be crouching. They could be running. You have to respond to all these behaviors that humans could potentially exhibit on these sites, along with the variety of variations in human appearance, you know, clothes, size, shape, height, skin color, everything else.”
It’s still early days for both Safeworld and generative AI in robotics, and the company is still figuring out the best model for its product — a platform for external users, or a services-based approach? — but the team is confident they are taking on the right problem.
“We’ll probably be the first profitable company in this field,” Zaho says. “Because if anyone wants to deploy, they need to pay us to handle the situation.”

title_en: Google's Fitbit Edge leaks out with a screen and Pixel 11 colors
title_fa: Google's Fitbit Edge leaks out with a screen and Pixel 11 colors
excerpt_en: The upcoming Fitbit Edge looks like a replacement for the Fitbit Charge last seen in 2023.
excerpt_fa: The upcoming Fitbit Edge looks like a replacement for the Fitbit Charge last seen in 2023.
content_en:
Google's Fitbit Edge leaks out with a screen and Pixel 11 colors
It could offer a seven-day battery life, altimeter and limited support for apps like Google Maps.
We knew that Google was likely coming out with a mid-range Fitbit model that slots between the Fitbit Air and the Pixel Watch 5, thanks to ads that surfaced earlier this year. Now we're seeing the first leak of the upcoming fitness tracker called the Fitbit Edge thanks to Android Headlines. It could be a replacement for the Fitbit Charge last seen in 2023, as it's equipped with a similar small screen and expected to have features like a GPS and notifications.
The leaks suggest that the Fitbit Edge will offer a seven-day battery life, GPS, altimeter and limited app support for apps like Google Maps and YouTube music. That will make it a more powerful Fitbit Air or a Pixel Watch 5 "lite," but one that runs on iOS as well as Android, unlike the Android-only Watch 5.
